title: Foundation: get_backend ignores fixtures= under live mode, so a deliberately-offline backend built through it would attempt a real API call
body:
## The sharp edge

`get_backend(fixtures=...)` **ignores `fixtures` entirely when `JEV_COOKBOOK_LIVE=1`**. From the function itself:

```python
live = os.environ.get(LIVE_ENV, "")
...
if live == "1":
    return _make_live_backend(fixtures=fixtures, script=script, seed=seed)
```

The docstring states it plainly — *"`JEV_COOKBOOK_LIVE=1` selects the live backend and **never falls back to replay**"* — and that behaviour is right for the backend a recipe wants to become live.

**But it means `get_backend` is the wrong constructor for a backend that must stay offline**, and nothing says so. A recipe comparing Jev against fabricated adapters, using `get_backend(fixtures=...)` for each, would under live mode **attempt a real API call for a model that does not exist.**

## How it surfaced, and why this is a near-miss rather than a defect report

Recipe 50 (PR #289) compares `jev` against two fabricated adapters. Its builder identified this before writing the harness and built the fabricated adapters as **plain `ReplayBackend`s**, reserving `get_backend` for `jev` alone — precisely so that live mode would call the one backend that is meant to be callable. It reported the reasoning rather than only the code.

So nothing shipped wrong, and the builder judged — defensibly — that nothing in `backends.py` was *missing*. I am filing it anyway because the hazard is in the **absence of guidance**, not in the function:

- The next multi-backend recipe is **#55, "Adaptive model routing"**, which also carries `needs: live run`. It will face the identical choice.
- The failure mode is **invisible offline**. Every test, every CI leg and every notebook execution passes, because the branch only differs when `JEV_COOKBOOK_LIVE=1` — which no automated check sets.
- And the consequence crosses a standing project constraint: an unintended live call, for a model that does not exist, against a $25 grant that is currently untouched with coverage at 0/60.

## Suggested fix

**Documentation is probably enough, and it belongs in two places:**

1. **`get_backend`'s own docstring**: one sentence saying that `fixtures` is ignored under live mode, so a backend intended to remain offline should be constructed as `ReplayBackend(...)` / `ReplayBackend.from_json(...)` directly rather than through `get_backend`.
2. **`docs/backends.md` and/or `docs/live.md`**: the same point where a recipe author planning a multi-backend comparison will meet it.

**A guard is possible but probably the wrong shape.** A check could look for more than one `get_backend` call in a recipe, but that is a check keyed on a call count standing in for intent — the family this repository already tracks in #222, #227, #234, #270, #272, #276, #282 and #283. A recipe may legitimately call it once; whether a *second* backend should be live is a design fact the source does not carry. **Prefer the documentation, and record the decision against a guard rather than leaving it open.**

Worth considering as an alternative to either: an explicit keyword on `get_backend` — something that makes "this one is meant to go live" and "this one never does" different calls rather than the same call in different environments. That is a shared-code change and so a larger decision than this issue should settle alone.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `get_backend`'s docstring says `fixtures` is ignored under live mode and names the alternative for a deliberately-offline backend.
- [ ] The point appears where a multi-backend recipe author will meet it before writing the harness.
- [ ] A decision is recorded on whether anything enforces it, with reasons either way.

## Provenance

Found by recipe 50's builder while designing a three-backend harness, and avoided before any code was written. Verified independently here by reading `get_backend` against a fetched ref. Nothing is broken today; this is about the next author who does not happen to check.

**Credit where it belongs**: a second thing that builder got right for the same reason is worth recording beside this one. It kept the fabricated adapters' stored answers in **separate files** (`responses-atlas.json`, `responses-north.json`), leaving `responses.json` holding exactly the **41** entries a live run would bill — so the project's `requests == len(responses.json)` identity survives a recipe with backends that are never called live, instead of needing a paragraph to explain it away. That file split matching the billing boundary is the pattern a later multi-backend recipe should copy.

title: Foundation: give style.py a rendering-assertions test module — #267, #278 and #286 are one defect in three faces
body:
## One defect in three faces

Three issues currently sit in `src/jev_cookbook/style.py`, and the review that found the third named what they share:

- **#267** — `plot_risk_coverage` plots in input order with no sorting and no points-only mode, so ordering logic is pushed into every caller, where it has already collided with a guard and reddened a head.
- **#278** — `plot_confusion_matrix` truncates tick labels at 14 characters with no wrap or rotate, so two classes sharing a prefix would render identically. Benign today only because the truncated prefixes happen to stay unique.
- **#286** — `plot_answer_probabilities` draws its bar value label under the hardcoded `loc="lower right"` legend, on **exactly** the confident case, because `invert_yaxis()` makes the highest rubric level the bottom bar.

**The common cause: the figure is the only artefact in this repository verified by its existence and byte size rather than its content.** Every one of these three is invisible from the source, invisible to the test suite, and visible only to a human opening the committed PNG — which the contract requires but cannot enforce. Each was found by a reviewer decoding an image, and one mislabelled axis has already reached `main` by this route.

## The proposal: a rendering-assertions module, not three separate fixes

A small test module that renders a figure and asserts properties of the **rendered artists** would catch all three classes and any future member, needs only a renderer, and involves **no image diffing, no golden files, and nothing version-fragile**. The three assertions that cover the known cases:

1. **No two text artists' bounding boxes intersect.** Catches #286 and any future collision between a label, a legend, an annotation or a tick.
2. **Each tick label's rendered text equals its source string.** Catches #278 **by construction** rather than at one particular length — a check keyed on label *length* cannot see a prefix collision, while one keyed on the rendered text cannot miss it.
3. **Axis titles match the vocabulary of the data plotted on that axis.** The shape of #267's problem, and of the mislabelled axis that reached `main`.

That is a renderer-only test: `fig.canvas.draw()` then `get_window_extent()` on the artists. Stable across matplotlib versions in a way image comparison is not, and it asserts the property rather than a snapshot.

## Why consolidate rather than fix three times

Fixing each issue separately leaves the **class** open: the next figure defect will be a fourth face of the same thing, found again by a reviewer with a decoder, after it has shipped. A module that owns the rendering invariants makes the figure a tested artefact instead of an attested one.

It also puts the check where the cost is low. Opening every committed PNG is currently a reviewer obligation discharged by hand, several times per recipe, and it has caught real defects — but it is the most expensive form of verification in the process and the least reliable, because it depends on a human noticing.

## Scope and sequencing

- This issue owns the module and the three assertions.
- **#286 should close into this** — its specific fix (a conditional legend corner, or a legend outside the axes) is worth doing, but the assertion is what prevents the next one.
- **#278 and #267 can be fixed independently**; assertion 2 makes #278's fix verifiable and assertion 3 bears on #267, so neither is blocked by this and both are strengthened by it.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A test module renders each plotting helper's output and asserts the three properties above.
- [ ] Each assertion is proved able to fail — plant a prefix collision, an overlapping label and a mismatched axis title, and watch the matching assertion redden.
- [ ] The known defects are covered: a confident `Score` answer (#286), a label set sharing eleven characters (#278).
- [ ] No golden images and no byte comparison, so the tests survive a matplotlib upgrade.

## Provenance

Proposed by the Opus review of PR #285, which had found #286 by opening the committed figures and was asked whether the module wanted a consolidated approach. Its answer, quoted because the framing is the useful part: *"#267, #278 and #286 are one defect in three faces: the figure is the only artefact verified by its existence and byte size rather than its content."*

title: Foundation: Notebook (37-research-domain-tagging) fails ~1 run in 4 on 'cell 2 wrote to stderr', taking Notebooks (execute) with it on unrelated PRs
body:
## The observation

`Notebook (37-research-domain-tagging)` fails intermittently with **"cell 2 (setup) wrote to stderr"**. Measured across four runs on **identical inputs** — recipe 37 was not in the diff of any of them:

| run | result |
|---|---|
| `main` at `5af4ab5` | pass |
| PR #281 round-2 head | pass |
| PR #281 round-3 head | **fail** |
| PR #281 approved head `56d93ab` | pass |

Three passes to one failure, same inputs throughout. **This is not a claim that recipe 37 is defective** — on this evidence it is not, and the reviewer that gathered it explicitly judged no main-side defect warranted. It is a claim about a **~1-in-4 observed failure rate in a stderr-write guard**, filed so the next person to meet it starts from the measurement rather than re-deriving it.

## Why it is worth tracking rather than ignoring

Two multipliers make this more expensive than a single flaky leg.

**It takes the aggregate with it.** `Notebooks (execute)` inherits the per-recipe leg, so one nondeterministic stderr write turns **two** checks red.

**And it lands on unrelated pull requests.** Every shared-code change on `main` widens each recipe pull request's notebook matrix to **all 48 published recipes plus the template** — so any recipe PR opened after a shared-code merge executes recipe 37, and has a ~1-in-4 chance of a red leg that has nothing to do with it. That already cost one review round the work of proving a red leg was not its own: gathering the three-pass comparison, checking main's own run, and re-reading a prior head's saved check list.

So the cost is not the flake, it is **the recurring diagnosis**, paid by whichever reviewer meets it next, with the default inference being the wrong one (a reviewer who assumes a red leg is theirs will go looking in the wrong recipe).

## What would settle it

- **Find the stderr write.** "Cell 2 (setup)" narrows it to that recipe's setup cell; a nondeterministic write there is most likely a library warning on a code path taken only sometimes — a cache state, a font cache rebuild, a thread or resource warning, a `numpy`/`matplotlib` first-use message. Running that cell repeatedly in a cold environment should reproduce it.
- **Decide what the guard should do about a warning it cannot attribute.** The guard is right to treat stderr as a failure by default; the question is whether a known, benign, nondeterministic warning should be matched and excluded **by exact text**, which is narrow and auditable, rather than the check being loosened.
- Until either happens, **record the measurement where a reviewer will find it**, which is what this issue is for.

**Do not weaken the stderr guard to make this pass.** That guard catches real defects, and "never weaken a check to pass it" is a standing rule here. An exact-text exclusion for one identified warning is not a weakening; raising the threshold or dropping the check is.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The stderr write is identified by text and cause, or the attempt to reproduce it is recorded as unsuccessful with what was tried.
- [ ] If an exclusion is added, it matches exact text and has a test proving an *unexpected* stderr write still fails.
- [ ] The observed failure rate is updated here as more runs accumulate, so a later reader can tell whether it got better or worse.

## Provenance

Measured by the Opus reviews of PR #281 across four rounds, which established the three-pass-to-one-failure comparison on identical inputs rather than inferring a flake from a single red leg. The matrix-widening multiplier was established separately on the same pull request, where a recipe-only diff produced 58 legs because `main` had gained shared-code changes.

title: Foundation: plot_answer_probabilities draws its bar value label under the hardcoded lower-right legend, on exactly the confident Score case
body:
## The defect

`src/jev_cookbook/style.py`, `plot_answer_probabilities`: bar value labels are drawn at `min(v, 1.0) + 0.015`, while the score legend is hardcoded to `loc="lower right"`.

After `invert_yaxis()`, **the highest rubric level is the bottom bar.** So for any `Score` answer whose highest level is also its most probable — the ordinary confident case, and the one a recipe is most likely to show a reader — that bar's value label is drawn at the far right of the bottom row, which is exactly where the legend box sits. The label lands **under the legend and across the dashed score line.**

Measured on recipe 49 (PR #285): **both** committed answer figures are affected, with `0.90` and `0.98` partly occluded.

## Why this is worth a ticket rather than a convention

**It is invisible from source.** Nothing in the plotting call, the data, or any test reveals it — the numbers are correct, the bars are correct, the legend is correct, and the overlap exists only in the rendered raster. The only way to see it is to open the committed PNG, which this project requires but which cannot be enforced mechanically.

**And it is set-wide and systematic**, not a one-recipe accident: it fires precisely on the *confident* case, so the clearer a recipe's example answer, the more likely its figure is damaged. Every `Score` recipe that shows a high-confidence answer is exposed, and more are scheduled.

A mislabelled or occluded axis inside a committed figure has already reached `main` once in this project and was caught only by a reviewer decoding the PNG.

## Suggested fix, in preference order

1. **Choose the legend corner conditionally** — place it away from the row carrying the longest or rightmost label, which the function already knows because it is drawing those labels.
2. **Move the legend out of the axes** (`bbox_to_anchor`), which removes the class of collision rather than this instance of it.
3. Failing either, **offset the value label inward** for the bar nearest the legend.

Add a test that renders a confident `Score` answer — highest level most probable — and asserts the value-label artist's bounding box does not intersect the legend's. That is checkable in matplotlib without comparing images, and it is the only form that would have caught this: a test keyed on the *data* or on the *call* cannot see a layout collision.

## Related

- **#278** — `plot_confusion_matrix` truncates tick labels at 14 characters with no wrap or rotate. Same module, same shape: a rendering limitation invisible from source, benign until two classes share a prefix.
- **#267** — `plot_risk_coverage` neither sorts nor offers a points-only mode, so ordering logic is pushed into every caller.

Three findings now sit in `style.py`, all of the same kind: the figure is content, and nothing in the test suite reads it. Worth considering whether the module wants a small rendering-assertions test module of its own rather than three separate fixes.

## Provenance

Found by the Opus review of PR #285, which opened both committed figures rather than reading the plotting source, and identified the `invert_yaxis()` interaction that makes the confident case the affected one.

title: Foundation: an empty notebook matrix produces no per-recipe leg at all, so a missing clean-kernel execution is indistinguishable from a passing one
body:
## "No leg" is indistinguishable from "leg green" on the checks list

`Notebook (<recipe>)` is a **per-recipe job name**, produced from a matrix, not a fixed required check. And `tools/notebook_ci.py`'s `execute` step is gated on `count != '0'`.

So **an empty matrix produces no job at all** — and on a pull request's checks list, a check that was never created looks exactly like a check that passed. Nothing is red, nothing is pending, and the merge gate sees a clean list.

This is the skipped-check family at the CI level, and it is the quietest instance of it in the repository: a skipped *test* at least contributes a line of `s` to pytest output. A missing *leg* contributes nothing.

## Reachability

The matrix basis is already the safer of the two options — `tools/notebook_ci.py` uses a **three-dot** diff from `pull_request.base.sha` for pull requests, with explicit "run everything" fall-backs for forced pushes and rewritten history. The failure mode is not a wrong basis; it is an **empty selection**.

An empty selection is reachable whenever a recipe's change is **already present at the merge base** — a cherry-pick, the same content arriving by another route, or a branch rebuilt on top of a commit that already carries it. The diff is then genuinely empty for that recipe, the matrix is empty, no `Notebook (<slug>)` job is created, and the per-recipe clean-kernel execution — which is the check that a notebook's committed outputs actually reproduce — **silently does not happen.**

Measured context from the review that found this: on one recipe pull request the leg count went from **10 to 57** between two heads with a recipe-only diff, because `main` had moved and carried shared-code paths into the comparison. That direction is **benign** — more coverage. The same mechanism in the other direction produces fewer legs, and at the limit, none.

## Suggested fix: assert the matrix is non-empty rather than change the basis

Do **not** change the diff basis — the three-dot comparison against `base.sha` is correct, and the run-everything fall-backs are the right defaults.

Instead add the positive assertion:

> A pull request whose diff touches `recipes/NN-*/notebook.ipynb` must produce a **non-empty** matrix.

That fails closed on the one case that matters, costs one check, and leaves the basis alone. It is the same shape as the fix proposed in #282 — a small positive requirement that makes an existing skip condition sound, rather than widening the condition itself.

Consider also whether `Notebooks (execute)`'s own gate should distinguish "nothing to execute because nothing changed" from "nothing to execute because the selection was computed wrongly". The first is correct behaviour; the second is this issue.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A pull request touching a recipe's `notebook.ipynb` with an empty computed matrix **fails**, proved by constructing that case rather than reasoning about it.
- [ ] A pull request touching no notebook still passes with an empty matrix, so the guard does not fire on the legitimate case.
- [ ] The failure message says which recipe was expected and why, rather than naming a count.

## Provenance

Found by the Opus review of PR #281, which investigated an unexplained 10→57 leg count, established the widening direction as benign, and then asked the sharper question — what happens in the other direction. The basis and fall-backs were read from `tools/notebook_ci.py` rather than inferred.

Family: #222, #227, #234, #249, #270, #272, #276, #282 — a check keyed on a correlate, or absent, standing in for a property. #249 is the closest relative: it fixed skip conditions keyed on `responses.json` rather than on the property each check meant, and recorded that **a skipped check is the quietest kind of gap**. A missing leg is quieter still.

title: Foundation: multi-proposition Noul issues do not require positives, truth combinations, or an outcome-determining row — the requirement only reaches builders via briefs
body:
## The gap

Recipe 48's issue (#48) asks for a `Noul` that "checks each selection for consistency with the paragraph context", and lists two propositions by implication. **It does not ask for the four truth combinations**, nor for positives of each proposition in the split used to select thresholds, nor for a row where each proposition's tag determines an outcome.

That requirement reached the builder **only through an orchestration brief**. The issue itself is silent, so a builder working from the issue alone — which is what the contract asks — has no reason to construct them.

What the review of #281 measured as a result:

- `introduces_new_fact`'s positives were **two slot-for-slot paraphrases of one hand-written sentence**, which leaked the label into surface form: a bare `"%" in text` scored **1.0000 with zero false positives on validation** and transferred to test.
- `breaks_reference` had **zero gold positives in validation**, one in test that the stored answer misses, **no row where its tag determines an outcome**, and **no both-true row anywhere**.
- So the recipe's declared limitation — that `select_threshold` could not choose a threshold from examples because an F1 sweep was degenerate — was a **symptom** of the fixture gap rather than an independent limitation.

None of that is a builder error. Every one of those properties follows from what the issue did not say.

## Why this is the #26 pattern in a new form

#26's amendment recorded the inverse: *listing as many fixture groups as there are labels produces labels that cannot disagree*, so an issue must **name the mixed and neither cases explicitly**. That guidance currently lives in #26's history and in an orchestration brief.

This is the same defect with **no** fixture groups listed rather than too few. An issue that names the propositions but not their combinations leaves the hardest and most informative rows — both true, both false, each true alone — to chance.

## It will recur, and the recipes are already scheduled

Two unbuilt recipes have a multi-proposition `Noul` in their design: **#53** and **#56**. Both will reach their builders the same way #48 did, and the same gap will reproduce unless the requirement is in the issue.

## What to do

1. **Amend #53 and #56 now**, before they are built, to require: a positive example of **every** proposition in the split used for threshold selection; at least one row per truth **combination** that the use case admits; and at least one row where **each** proposition's tag changes the composed outcome. The last is what makes a battery a battery rather than two questions that happen to share a request.
2. **Put the guidance where issues are written**, not only in a brief — the recipe-template or issue-template docs, so the next multi-proposition issue inherits it. The orchestration brief is the wrong home because it reaches builders rather than issue authors, and because an issue outlives the brief that supplemented it.
3. Consider whether a **guard** can express it: "for each `Noul` proposition in a recipe, at least one gold-true and one gold-false row in each scored split" is a mechanical property of `labels.jsonl` plus the question definitions. Note the usual caution — a check keyed on a proposition's **name** would be the seventh instance of the idiom-keyed family in this repository, so it must key on the question definitions the recipe actually builds.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] #53 and #56 carry the requirement before a builder is dispatched.
- [ ] The guidance lives in a document an issue author reads.
- [ ] A decision is recorded on whether a guard enforces it, with reasons either way.

## Provenance

Raised by the Opus review of PR #281 as an out-of-scope finding, with every figure above measured on the committed fixtures rather than predicted.

title: Foundation: nothing requires a recipe's confidence gate to come from the shared helper, so a hardcoded gate SKIPS three checks instead of failing them
body:
## The gap

Nothing in the recipe guard requires a recipe's confidence gate to come from the shared helper. Three checks all key on finding a **resolvable call** to `select_confidence_threshold(` / `select_threshold(`, and each **skips** when it finds none:

- `threshold_objective_pin` — skips when no resolvable call is found (since #244 / #273).
- `stored_answers_strong_form` (`G1(c)`) — skips when no resolvable call is found (as of #280, which re-keyed it on "does this recipe freeze a threshold at all", correctly replacing a worse correlate).
- `review_reason_string` — only substring-searches `helpers.py`.

So a recipe that freezes a gate as a **bare constant** (`GATE = 0.85`) or through an **attribute-style call** the finder does not resolve is invisible to all three. It does not fail them; it **skips** them, which is the quietest possible outcome and reads as a pass.

**Zero recipes are affected today** — measured across all 47 published folders by the reviewer of #280, which also measured the inverse: a hardcoded gate or an attribute-style call turns what used to be a clean FAIL into a SKIP.

## Why this is worth a positive check rather than a wider skip condition

#280 made those skip conditions name the **property** rather than a correlate, which was the right fix and is why this gap is now visible: once a skip says "does this recipe freeze a threshold at all", the question "what if it freezes one in a way we cannot see?" becomes answerable.

The honest answer is that the guard cannot detect every way a gate might be frozen, and **widening the detector is the wrong direction** — this repository has five findings about checks keyed on source idioms, and #276 already tracks the enumerate-versus-derive problem in the adjacent machinery. Adding more accepted spellings to the finder would be the sixth instance.

**The right shape is a small positive check**: every recipe whose evaluation reports a gated or selective metric must freeze its threshold through the shared helper. That is a one-line property, it is enforceable, it fails closed on a recipe that hardcodes a gate, and it tells the author what to do rather than silently removing three checks. It also makes the three skip conditions above sound, because "no resolvable call" would then mean "no gate" rather than "a gate we cannot see".

Note the alternative that should **not** be chosen: making the skips fail closed on an unresolvable call would turn every genuinely gate-free recipe red. The distinction the guard needs is between *no gate* and *an unseen gate*, and only a positive requirement supplies it.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A recipe that freezes a gate as a bare constant is **caught**, proved by mutation on a published recipe that currently passes — convert its helper call to a constant and show the new check reddens.
- [ ] A recipe with genuinely no gate still passes, proved on whichever published recipe has none.
- [ ] The failure message names the requirement — use the shared helper — rather than naming a shape.
- [ ] The three skip conditions above are left as they are; this check is what makes them sound.

## Provenance

Found by the Opus review of PR #280 as an out-of-scope finding, with the zero-recipes-today figure and the FAIL→SKIP conversion both measured rather than predicted.

Family: #222, #227, #234, #270, #272, #276 — a check keyed on an idiom standing in for the property it means.

title: Foundation: plot_confusion_matrix truncates tick labels at 14 chars with no wrap or rotate, so two classes sharing a prefix would render identically
body:
## The limitation

`plot_confusion_matrix` in `src/jev_cookbook/style.py` shortens tick labels to **14 characters** — `_shorten(str(x), 14)` returns `text[:11].rstrip() + "..."` — with no wrapping, no rotation and no option to keep the full text. On a matrix with more than three or four classes and descriptive class names, several axis labels become ellipses.

Measured on recipe 47 (`#277`), a five-class matrix: `factual_disagreement` renders as `factual_dis…` and `not_conflicting` as `not_conflic…`.

**It is benign there, and the reason it is benign is the point**: the truncated prefixes happen to stay **unique**, so a reader can still tell the classes apart, and the printed table beside the figure carries the full names. That recipe's author opened the committed PNG, confirmed the truncation, and **disclosed it rather than renaming the options to dodge it** — which its reviewer ruled the right call, and I agree.

**The failure mode is when two classes share their first eleven characters.** Then two different rows or columns render identically and the figure becomes actively misleading rather than merely abbreviated. Nothing warns the author; nothing in CI checks it; and the committed PNG is content that a reader may trust over the table beside it. A mislabelled axis inside a committed figure has already got through every automated check on an earlier recipe in this project.

## Why this is worth fixing rather than conventioning around

The alternative is a rule telling recipe authors to keep class names under twelve characters, which fails for the same reason every naming convention in this repository has failed: it is a constraint on prose that nothing enforces, and the first author to need `factual_disagreement` will write it. Three recipes already carry class names that truncate.

The helper also already has the information needed to do better — it knows the label set, so it can detect a prefix collision and act.

## Suggested fix, in preference order

1. **Rotate or wrap** rather than truncate, so full labels survive; matplotlib supports both and the figure has the room on the vertical axis.
2. If truncation is kept as a fallback, **detect prefix collisions and raise** rather than render two identical ticks — fail closed on an ambiguous figure.
3. Optionally expose the width, so a recipe with long class names can choose.

Add a test with a label set whose members share their first eleven characters, asserting the rendered ticks are distinguishable (or that the call raises). Note the general hazard in this repository: a check keyed on a label's *length* will not notice a collision, and a check keyed on the *rendered* ticks will — so assert on what the figure actually carries.

## Related

- **#267** — `plot_risk_coverage` neither sorts nor offers a points-only mode, so ordering logic is pushed into every caller. Same helper module, same shape of problem: a limitation that each caller must work around, where the workaround meets checks the helper's author never considered.
- `plot_confusion_matrix` also takes a **single** `labels` list and sets `xlabel="Predicted"` / `ylabel="Gold"` unconditionally, which is worth noting in the same pass if the signature is being touched.

## Provenance

Raised by the Opus review of PR #277 as an out-of-scope finding, with the truncation measured on the committed figure rather than inferred from the source.

title: Foundation: the objective-pin check enumerates polarity instead of deriving it, so a spelling asserted ABSENT is credited as present
body:
## The remaining axis: polarity is enumerated, not derived

#273's objective-pin check now ties a credited spelling to a **tainted operand** — a value traced to a read of the real committed source — which is a property and closed the three spellings tracked in #275. It also tracks polarity through an enclosing `not` and through `and`/`or`.

**But the comparison walk yields an `ast.Compare` node and never descends into its operands.** So negation expressed as a **value** or by **context** is invisible, and a spelling asserted *absent* is credited as *present*. Measured in the review of `4db7722a`:

```python
assert ("target_accuracy" in source) is False      # credited
assert source.count("target_accuracy") == 0        # credited
assert len([m for m in … if "target_accuracy" in m]) == 0   # credited
assert ("target_accuracy" in source) if cond else True       # IfExp, credited
```

Each of those says the spelling is **not** there, and each is read as evidence that it is.

## Reachability, measured rather than assumed

- **`== False` is lint-blocked** by ruff **E712**, and an assert on a tuple by **F631** — both confirmed against this repository's own ruff configuration, so those two spellings cannot reach `main`.
- **`is False` and `count(…) == 0` are not blocked by any lint rule.** And `is False` is **already house idiom** here — recipes 14 and 15 use it repeatedly, just not yet on a membership test.
- **No live instance across all 46 published recipes.** This is latent, not active.

So the hazard is a spelling that is idiomatic in this repository, carries no lint protection, and would be read backwards by the guard the first time someone writes it on a membership test.

## The under-match side of the same gap

Taint does not reach a comprehension variable, so legitimate pins are **refused**:

```python
assert all("min_coverage" in s for s in sources)   # refused
assert any(…)                                       # refused
```

That is the same shape as the original blocking finding on #273 — a real pin rejected for how it is spelled — and it is the reason this issue is worth fixing properly rather than by adding `Is`-against-`False` to a blacklist.

## The fix

Derive polarity rather than enumerate it: evaluate the **effective truth sense** of the comparison in the context where its result is used, descending into operands so that a `Compare` nested inside another comparison, a `count(…) == 0`, an `IfExp` branch or a comprehension's `all`/`any` wrapper each contribute their sign. Equivalently: ask what the assert claims about the spelling, not which operators appear on the way there.

A blacklist of negative spellings is the wrong shape and this repository has the evidence: `CONTRIBUTING.md` section 6's spelling list has been evaded **five** times by different wordings, `_citation_hits` runs only two patterns (which is how six recipes drifted past it), and #273 itself went through three rounds precisely because each revision recognised one more idiom rather than the property.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Each of the four spellings above is **rejected**, proved by planting it in a recipe that currently passes and watching the check go red.
- [ ] `all(…)` and `any(…)` pins over a tainted source are **accepted**, proved by mutation on a recipe written that way.
- [ ] All shapes in use today still pass, proved by mutation on each rather than by inspection.
- [ ] The rejections and acceptances are covered by **committed tests** that fail when the fix is reverted — not hand-run probes.

## Provenance

Found by the Opus review of PR #273 at `4db7722a`, which approved that head while flagging this as a separate axis — on the reasoning that folding it in would make #275's title false about its contents, which was that issue's own subject. Filed separately for the same reason.

Family: #222, #227, #234, #270, #272 — a check keyed on a source idiom certifying the letter of a rule it cannot observe.

title: Foundation: the threshold-objective pin ties spelling to source at STATEMENT level, not OPERAND level — three spellings of one hole
body:
## The hole

#273's `threshold_objective_pin` check credits `assert <string literal> in <name>` inside a test function whose own source text shows it reads the committed notebook or `helpers.py`. Its reviewer planted a **tautological pin** in recipe 01 and the check **accepted it** (reported as `[XPASS(strict)]`): an assertion whose two sides are both known at authoring time satisfies the shape without the recipe reading anything that would change if the real call were edited.

So the property that matters — *a keyword swap in the real committed call makes something in this recipe's tests fail* — is not established by the shape the check looks for. A recipe can satisfy the check and still ship a byte-identical notebook with a false printed objective line, which is the exact defect #244 exists to prevent.

## Why this is conditional on how #273's blocking finding is fixed

#273's review found the check **refuses four recipes that have real pins** (28, 41, 42, 44 — plus recipe 46 on its open PR), because it recognises only one spelling of the evidence: only the `In` operator, and only a committed-source read that sits **inside the audited test function's own source segment**.

There are two ways to fix that:

1. **Widen the recognised shapes** — accept `==`, `.count(...) == n`, a negative `not in`, an f-string literal, a behavioural assertion through `helpers`, and a read performed by a module-level helper.
2. **Trace the tie** — establish that some assertion depends on a value that came from reading the real committed source, however the read is spelled and wherever it lives. The module already has `_labelled_names`/`_derived_from` machinery doing data-flow work for other checks.

**If #273 takes route 1, this issue stays open and needs its own fix.** Widening the shapes makes the check accept more spellings of the evidence *and* more spellings of a tautology, and the per-function scoping — the one thing standing between the check and a hand-rolled string — is already measured not to close the hole. If #273 takes route 2, a traced read-to-assertion tie would close this by construction, and this issue can be closed with that as the reason.

## Family

Same family as #222 (the strong-form guard), #227 (the reason-string guard), #234 (the validation-metric-line guard), #270 (`FLOAT_FORMAT` and `METRIC_KEYWORD` failing in opposite directions on adjacent lines) and #272 (`_find_function_body`'s decorator blindness): **a check keyed on a source idiom certifies the letter of a rule it cannot observe.** That is now six findings of the same shape, and #273 would be the seventh if it recognises a widened list of idioms rather than the property.

The generalisation already recorded in this project is that enumerating spellings is the wrong shape of defence — `CONTRIBUTING.md` section 6's list has been evaded five times by different wordings, and `_citation_hits` runs only two patterns, which is how six recipes drifted past it.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A tautological pin — one whose assertion cannot fail when the real committed call changes — is rejected, with a failure message that says what is missing rather than naming a shape.
- [ ] The rejection is proved by mutation: plant a tautological pin in a recipe that currently passes and show the check goes red.
- [ ] The check still accepts all five spellings real recipes use today (28, 41, 42, 44, 46), proved by mutation on each rather than by inspection.

## Provenance

Raised by the Opus review of PR #273 as an out-of-scope item, explicitly conditioned on how that PR's blocking finding is resolved. The tautological pin was planted and the acceptance measured rather than argued.

title: Foundation: sum() over floats is not bit-stable across CPython 3.12, so a byte-exact fixture assertion can pass on one Tests leg and fail the other
body:
## The hazard

**CPython 3.12 changed `sum()` to use Neumaier compensated summation for floats.** This repository's two test legs — `Tests (py3.10)` and `Tests (py3.14)` — straddle that change, and **45 recipes assert that their committed `fixtures/responses.json` is byte-identical to a fresh `build_responses(ROWS)`**. So any fixture builder that computes a stored float through `sum()` can pass on one leg and fail on the other.

Measured on Python 3.11.2:

```
sum([1.0, 0.35, 0.1225, 0.042875])  -> 1.5153750000000001
left-to-right loop                  -> 1.5153750000000001   (agrees)
math.fsum(...)                      -> 1.515375             (the compensated value)
```

On 3.12+ `sum()` returns `1.515375`. A hand-written accumulation loop agrees on both sides; `sum()` does not agree with itself across the boundary.

**`float ** int` is a second, independent instance of the same class.** CPython routes `float.__pow__` to the platform's libm `pow()`, whose last-bit accuracy is not guaranteed across builds. `0.5 ** k` is exact (power of two); `0.08 ** k` and `0.35 ** k` are not.

## How it surfaced

Recipe 46 (PR #271) went red on `Tests (py3.10)` while `Tests (py3.14)` was green, failing the byte-exact assertion with 1-ulp differences:

```
-           "1": 0.23096593252495254,
+           "1": 0.23096593252495257,
```

Its builder reproduced the failure on a real 3.10 interpreter, fixed the `**` call, found the test **still red**, and isolated `sum()` as a second independent cause. Both are now replaced with exactly-specified equivalents in that recipe.

Note that this is **not** a defect in the byte-exact test, which is the right check and is portable: 45 recipes carry it and pass. The non-portability is in the arithmetic.

## Current exposure, measured against `origin/main`

**9 of 46** `build_fixtures.py` files call `sum(`. Of those:

- **Exposed in principle — summing floats with no rounding on that line:** `08-faq-selection`, `11-clarification-selection`, `13-candidate-rewrite-selection`, `18-duplicate-incident-matching`, `22-cmdb-asset-matching`, all via `remainder = 1.0 - sum(given.values())`.
- **Neutralised by rounding:** `24-incident-priority-composition` (`round(..., 2)`), `33-schema-field-mapping` (`round(..., 10)`). A 1-ulp difference does not survive either.
- **Not executed:** `32-regression-test-selection` — its `sum(` is inside a **string literal** of example test code.
- **Immune:** `34-evidence-relationship-labels` sums `len(...)`, i.e. integers.

**All five exposed recipes pass today, and the reason is worth recording:** compensated and naive summation **agree when there are fewer than three addends**. A pinned distribution with one or two given options cannot show the difference. The hazard is latent, not live — its trigger is three or more float addends with cancellation.

## What to do

1. **Document it** where fixture builders are written — `docs/fixtures.md` and `docs/recipe-template.md` — as a short rule: in a fixture builder whose output is byte-exact asserted, use only exactly-specified float operations. A left-to-right accumulation loop instead of `sum()`; repeated multiplication instead of `**`. Rounding the stored value also works, but prefer determinism in the construction over truncation of the output, since rounding hides the problem rather than removing it.
2. **Consider a guard.** A check that no `build_fixtures.py` calls `sum()` or `**` on floats would be cheap, but note the usual trap: a text-level check cannot tell `sum(len(x) for x in …)` from `sum(probabilities)`, and `32`'s hit is inside a string literal. An AST-based check that distinguishes them is possible; a regex is not, and this repository has five separate findings about checks keyed on source idioms certifying the letter. If a guard is written it should be AST-based and should state its requirement in the failure message.
3. **Decide whether to migrate the five exposed recipes** pre-emptively or leave them until one actually breaks. They are correct today; the argument for migrating is that the failure is confusing when it arrives and lands on whoever next edits those fixtures, not on whoever wrote the fragile line.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The rule is written where a builder writing `build_fixtures.py` will meet it.
- [ ] A decision is recorded on the five exposed recipes, either migrated or deliberately left with the reason.
- [ ] If a guard is added, it is AST-based, distinguishes integer from float summation, ignores string literals, and names its requirement in the failure message.

## Provenance

Found by recipe 46's builder during PR #271's fix round, by building a real 3.10 interpreter after the orchestrator's brief had asserted — **incorrectly** — that `sum()` is "exactly specified by IEEE-754 and bit-identical on every build". Each individual addition is so specified; `sum()` is a reduction whose algorithm is a CPython implementation choice, and that choice changed in 3.12. The builder had propagated the false claim into a code comment before measuring it, then corrected the comment to state the counterexample. Exposure set measured independently here.

title: Foundation: _find_function_body does not stop at a decorator, so a decorated neighbour makes the strong-form guard fail with an unrelated SyntaxError
body:
## What is wrong

`_find_function_body` (`tests/test_recipe_guard.py:377`) extracts a test function's body by scanning forward to the next top-level definition:

```python
next_def = re.search(r"\n(?:def |class )", body)
return def_line + (body[: next_def.start()] if next_def else body)
```

A **decorator line** is not `def ` or `class `, so it does not terminate the scan. When the audited function is immediately followed by a decorated function — the overwhelmingly common case in this repository, since `@pytest.mark.parametrize` is everywhere — the decorator lines are **folded into the extracted body**, and the subsequent `ast.parse` raises `SyntaxError`.

Reproduced minimally:

```
extracted body ends with:
'_all_right():\n    assert wrong_count > 0\n\n\n@pytest.mark.parametrize("x", [1, 2])'
ast.parse SyntaxError: invalid syntax (<unknown>, line 5)
```

## Why this is worse than a skip

The failure is **attributed to the wrong thing**. A recipe whose pin is perfectly correct gets a red check whose message is a `SyntaxError` about a line the recipe author did not write, in a function they are not being audited on. It is a false negative wearing the costume of a real finding — and a builder's natural response is to rearrange their own test file until the error goes away, which is what happened: recipe 46's builder worked around it by ordering its test file to avoid the pattern, documented the workaround in a comment, and correctly declined to touch shared test code.

So the guard currently imposes an **undocumented constraint on test-file layout** — "do not put a decorated function immediately after the audited one" — that no contract states and no reader could infer from the error.

## Fix

Terminate the scan at a decorator as well as at a definition, at column zero:

```python
next_def = re.search(r"\n(?:@|def |class )", body)
```

and add a regression test with the audited function followed by a `@pytest.mark.parametrize`-decorated one, asserting the extracted body parses. Include the negative case — a decorator *inside* the body (nested function) must not terminate the scan early — since `\n@` at column zero and an indented `@` are different things and the fix must distinguish them.

## Scope

Unknown how many recipes are affected, and I am deliberately not estimating: the answer depends on each recipe's test-file ordering, and an approximate regex over test files is exactly the class of instrument that has produced several wrong conclusions in this repository. The honest way to find out is to apply the fix and see which checks change verdict — which is cheap, because the fix is one character class.

Note that a recipe arranged to avoid the bug today has no marker saying so, so this also silently constrains future edits to those files: reordering a test file can turn a green check red with a `SyntaxError`.

## Provenance

Found by recipe 46's builder as an out-of-scope finding during PR #271, reported in its PR body rather than only in a code comment. Independently reproduced here.

Adjacent, already filed: #270 (`FLOAT_FORMAT` misses aligned format specs, and `METRIC_KEYWORD`'s `\bcoverage\b` cannot match inside `min_coverage` — two regexes failing in opposite directions on adjacent lines). Same family: a check keyed on a source idiom that cannot observe the property it stands for.

title: Foundation: FLOAT_FORMAT misses aligned format specs, so metric-line guards silently skip an aligned baselines table
body:
## What is wrong

`FLOAT_FORMAT` in `tests/test_recipe_guard.py:491` is

```python
FLOAT_FORMAT = re.compile(r"\{[^{}]*:\.\d+f\}")
```

The `:\.` requires the precision to sit **immediately** after the colon, so the regex matches `{x:.4f}` but **not** an aligned or width-bearing spec:

```
'{x:.4f}'      -> True
'{x:>13.4f}'   -> False
'{x:<8.2f}'    -> False
'{x:^10.4f}'   -> False
```

Two guards key off it — `test_validation_metric_lines_carry_selection_and_check` (check 4a) and `test_every_printed_metric_line_carries_at_least_check`. A printed metric line whose numbers use an aligned spec is therefore **not recognised as a metric line at all**, so neither guard ever evaluates it. The checks do not fail; they silently have nothing to say.

## Where it bites today

Exactly one published notebook, measured against `origin/main` (`aca7f32`):

```
$ git grep -l -E ':[<>^][0-9]+\.[0-9]+f' origin/main -- 'recipes/*/notebook.ipynb'
origin/main:recipes/43-failure-recovery-selection/notebook.ipynb
```

Its `evaluation-baselines` cell prints the baselines table as an aligned table:

```python
print(f"{'always retry':<28} {0:>8} {always_raw:>13.4f} {always_task.accuracy:>20.4f}{check}")
```

So the three lines that carry recipe 43's headline comparison — the ones the guard exists to police — are invisible to it. **No defect ships from this today**: those lines do carry `{check}`, by the author's own care rather than by enforcement. The gap is that nothing would have caught it had they not.

The same command shape with an unaligned spec (`:\.[0-9]+f`) hits **45** files, which is the can-speak proof that the search is working rather than silently empty.

## Why this is worth fixing rather than noting

An aligned table is the *natural* way to print a multi-row comparison, and multi-row comparisons are exactly where the `{check}` and `{selection}` labels matter most — a baselines table is the densest concentration of unlabelled-metric risk in any recipe. The guard's coverage is therefore weakest precisely where the contract is most load-bearing. As more Level 4 and 5 recipes print baseline tables, more of them will adopt the aligned form and silently leave the guard's scope.

This is the fail-open family catalogued in the briefs: **a check keyed on a source idiom certifies the letter**, and a sweep that fails open looks exactly like a clean sweep. Five guards have now been found with this shape.

## Suggested fix

Widen the spec to allow an optional format-spec prefix before the precision, e.g.

```python
FLOAT_FORMAT = re.compile(r"\{[^{}]*:[^{}]*\.\d+f\}")
```

and add a test that pins the widened behaviour on the aligned forms above — including a negative case, so the regex cannot quietly become everything-matching later. Re-running the two guards after widening will show whether any currently-skipped line also lacks its labels; recipe 43's do not, so the expected outcome is no new failures, which is worth confirming rather than assuming.

## Provenance

Found by the Opus-reviewed sweep builder on PR #269 (Level 4 prose sweep) as an out-of-scope finding — correctly out of its allowed paths, since the fix is in `tests/` and a recipe sweep's diff must stay inside `recipes/`. Independently reproduced here, including the one-file scope claim and the can-speak proof.

title: Foundation: plot_risk_coverage joins points in input order with no sorting and no points-only mode, so a mechanism-vs-baselines figure draws a zig-zag implying a frontier
body:
`plot_risk_coverage` joins its points with `ax.plot(x, y)` in **input order**, with **no sorting** and **no points-only mode**. For a monotone `SelectiveCurve` — which is what 29 of its 30 call sites pass — that is exactly right. For a handful of unordered points, such as a mechanism plotted against its baselines, it draws a **zig-zag line through a scatter**, and the figure then implies a frontier that does not exist.

Found by the Opus review of PR #266 (recipe 44), which **decoded the committed PNG** and saw it.

## Verified

`src/jev_cookbook/style.py:766-810`:

- the signature takes `coverage` and `risk` as *"aligned 1-D arrays"*, or any object with `.coverage` and `.risk` such as `SelectiveCurve`;
- the body is `x = _as_1d(coverage, …)`, `y = _as_1d(risk, …)`, then **`ax.plot(x, y, label=label)`**;
- grepping the whole function for `sort` or `argsort`: **no sorting anywhere**.

**30 call sites across 30 recipes on `main`**, and the ones visible in a grep all pass a `curve` — a `SelectiveCurve` produced by the evaluation toolkit, whose coverage is monotone by construction. So the helper's behaviour has been correct for every use until now.

Recipe 44 is the first to plot **discrete policies** on the same axes: it passed `reject_all` (coverage 1.0000), the mechanism (0.8667) and `approve_all` (1.0000) in that order, and the committed figure is a zig-zag. Its prose also claimed the points were *"plotted at ascending coverage"*, which the figure refutes — that claim is one of its must-changes, and this issue is the shared-code reason it was easy to write.

**Recipe 41 uses the same form** and happens to pass its points in ascending order, so its figure is fine today. That is a coincidence of input order, not a property anything enforces.

## Why it is worth closing

- **A line between unordered points asserts something.** A reader sees a frontier — a trade-off curve — where the author plotted three independent policies. That is a stronger misreading than a missing figure, and like the axis-label defect found on a sibling recipe, it lives in **pixels** and survives every source-level check.
- **The use case is now recurring.** Level 4 recipes compare a mechanism against structurally-determined baselines as a matter of course, and rule 19 in the house brief *requires* cost-and-coverage comparisons. So the handful-of-points use will keep arriving, and each recipe will solve it locally or not notice.
- It is a few lines.

## Suggested fix

Either sort by coverage before plotting, or add a points-only mode (`connect: bool = True`, or a `marker`/`linestyle` passthrough) so a caller with unordered policies can plot markers without an implied curve. Sorting is the smaller change and is harmless for a monotone curve; a points-only mode is more honest for the discrete case, since even sorted policy points are not a frontier.

Worth deciding which, because they say different things: a sorted line still claims the points lie on one curve.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Plotting unordered points produces a figure that does not imply a curve through them, proved by decoding the rendered PNG rather than by reading the call.
- [ ] All 30 existing call sites render **byte-identically** — 30 recipes commit one of these figures and a plotter change must not move them.
- [ ] A decision is recorded on sort-versus-points-only, with its reason.
- [ ] Recipe 41's figure is checked under whatever lands, since its correctness today rests on input order rather than on the helper.

title: Foundation: plot_confusion_matrix truncates tick labels to 14 chars with no collision check — two labels sharing 11 characters would render as the same tick
body:
`plot_confusion_matrix` shortens every tick label to 14 characters with **no collision check**, so two classes agreeing on their first 11 characters would render as the **same tick** on both axes — a figure that silently misattributes rows and columns, with the committed PNG looking entirely normal.

Raised by the Opus review of PR #263, which found it while reading `style.py` and deliberately did not audit the calling recipes. **I have done that audit; the result is below.**

## The mechanism

`src/jev_cookbook/style.py:615`:

```python
names = [_shorten(str(x), 14) for x in labels]
```

and `_shorten` (line 553):

```python
def _shorten(text: str, width: int = 28) -> str:
    return text if len(text) <= width else text[: width - 3].rstrip() + "..."
```

So any label longer than 14 characters becomes its **first 11 characters** plus `...`. Two labels sharing those 11 characters collapse to one identical tick, and the same `names` list is used for both axes.

## Audited: a latent trap, not a backlog

Measured across the published set at `86d4c11` (43 recipes), taking each label vocabulary from the **confusion-matrix table printed in the same cell** as the plot call — the committed output, not a regex over source constants — and applying a transcription of `_shorten` self-tested against its documented behaviour (`"abcdefghijklmnopq"` → `"abcdefghijk..."`, short strings unchanged):

- **55 cells** call `plot_confusion_matrix`;
- **0 recipes** have a label vocabulary that collides at 14 characters.

So nothing is wrong in the published set today, and this needs no cleanup sweep. It is the same shape as two other findings in this backlog — a figureless recipe satisfying both plot guards by vacuity, and the hoisted-format blind spot in the validation-metric-line guard — where an audit came back clean and established a **latent trap** rather than a debt. That is the useful thing to know when prioritising: the fix is cheap and there is nothing queued behind it.

## Why it is still worth closing

- **The failure is silent and lands in a committed artefact.** A sibling recipe shipped a confusion matrix whose x axis contradicted the table beside it, and it was found only because a reviewer decoded the PNG. A tick collision would be strictly harder to spot, because the axis *text* would look plausible — two rows simply labelled the same.
- **Label vocabularies are growing.** Level 4 recipes compose several stages and name their outcomes accordingly; `alternative_method` is already 18 characters, and `thread_previously_held`-style outcomes are the natural next step. The margin that keeps the current set clean is not something any check preserves.
- It is a few lines to fix.

## Suggested fix

Detect the collision and widen rather than truncate: if shortening produces duplicates, fall back to the full labels (or to the shortest prefix length that keeps them distinct). A one-line `len(set(names)) != len(names)` guard covers it, and a test with two labels sharing 11 characters pins it.

Worth deciding at the same time whether a silent truncation is right at all for an axis label — a rotated or wrapped full label may be better than an abbreviated one — but that is a presentation call and the collision is a correctness one.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Two labels sharing their first 11 characters render as **distinct** ticks, proved by a test that fails before the fix.
- [ ] All 55 existing call sites render unchanged — the published figures must stay byte-identical, since 43 recipes commit one and a plotter change must not move them.
- [ ] A decision is recorded on whether truncation remains the default presentation.

title: Foundation: full-suite totals differ by ~60 tests depending on the optional live extra, and a module-level importorskip hides it behind one SKIPPED line
body:
Two honest full-suite runs of the same tree differ by about **60 passes and 2 skips** depending on whether the optional `live` extra is installed — and the difference is invisible, because a **module-level `importorskip`** collapses an entire file into a single `SKIPPED` line. So a reported total like "3891 passed" and "3951 passed" can both be correct for the same commit, and neither figure says which set was measured.

Raised by the Opus review of PR #260, which reconciled the two by measurement rather than assuming one was wrong.

## Verified mechanism

- `tests/test_live_sdk.py:14-15` calls `pytest.importorskip("typesafe_sdk")` and `importorskip("httpx2")` at **module level**, so without the extra the whole file is one skip. It holds **19** test functions before parametrisation.
- `tests/test_notebook_ci_netguard.py:176` has an in-test `importorskip` for the same package.
- `.github/workflows/ci.yml` installs `.[dev]` on the 3.10 leg (line 35) and `.[dev,live]` on 3.14 (line 77), so **CI's own two legs legitimately differ by this amount** — which is correct behaviour, not a defect.

The review measured the gap precisely: those two files collect **78** tests with a stub on `PYTHONPATH` and **19** without — exactly 60 tests and 2 skips, reconciling `3891 / 7 / 42` against `3951 / 5 / 42`.

## Why it is worth a mechanism rather than care

This has cost reconciliation work **three times in one session**, each time looking briefly like a regression:

- `3702` against `3762` on one recipe's two rounds;
- `3819` against `3820` on another;
- `3891` against `3951` here.

Every one was resolved by hand, and every one *looked* like an unexplained change in test count — which is precisely the shape of a real problem. The cost is not the arithmetic; it is that **an unexplained +60 is indistinguishable from something going wrong**, so each occurrence consumes a reviewer's attention before being dismissed.

It is also the same shape as two traps already recorded in this project's house rules: a **paged list's default limit read as a count**, and a **missing wrapper command** that makes a comparison trivially pass. In all three, a believable number silently describes a different thing than the reader assumes. A plausible wrong answer is worse than an obviously broken one.

## Options

1. **Have the suite report how many tests were SDK-gated.** A `conftest.py` summary line — "60 tests skipped: optional `live` extra not installed" — makes the difference visible at the point of reading, and costs nothing when the extra is present. This is the cheapest fix and the only one that helps a reader who was not expecting the issue.
2. **Record expected totals both ways** wherever totals are quoted (receipts, briefs, the development docs), so a figure can be checked against the right baseline. Helps, but relies on everyone quoting the pair.
3. **Replace the module-level `importorskip` with per-test skips** so the skip count reflects the number of tests not run. Most faithful to pytest's own reporting, at the cost of 19 skip lines instead of 1.

Option 1 plus a note in the development docs looks like the best ratio; option 3 is worth considering on its own merits since a single `SKIPPED` standing for 19 tests is misleading regardless of this issue.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A reader of a bare `pytest` summary can tell whether the `live` extra was present, without counting.
- [ ] The expected totals for both installs are recorded where totals are compared, and kept current.
- [ ] A decision is recorded on the module-level `importorskip`, implemented or rejected with a reason.
- [ ] Whatever lands is proved by running the suite both ways and confirming the two reports are distinguishable **at a glance**.

title: Foundation: recipe files refer readers to "the build note" on a GitHub issue — 8 published recipes, and section 6 bans only #NNN and "the issue"
body:
Recipe files refer a reader to **"the build note"** — a section of the recipe's GitHub issue. A reader of the shipped repository cannot open it, which is exactly what `CONTRIBUTING.md` section 6 forbids for `#NNN` and "the issue", and for the same stated reason: *"a reader cannot see either."* The rule's illustrative list does not name this spelling, so it has spread.

Found by the Opus review of PR #260 (recipe 42), which also noted it had **missed the same thing in its own first round** on that recipe.

## Measured, with the criterion stated

Criterion: the case-insensitive substring **`build note`** (singular or plural, with or without a preceding "the") in any `.py`, `.md` or `.ipynb` under `recipes/` on `main` at `0ee89d8`, with notebooks searched by **cell source** only. Pattern self-tested against a planted sentence first.

**8 recipes, 9 files, 12 occurrences**: `03`, `05`, `06`, `15`, `18`, `19`, `22`, `29`.

Narrower spellings for comparison, since the criterion is what the count turns on:

| pattern | recipes | files | occurrences |
|---|---|---|---|
| `build note` (any form) | **8** | **9** | **12** |
| `the build note` | 5 | 6 | 7 |
| `build notes` (plural) | 4 | 5 | 5 |

I first measured the narrow form, got 5 recipes, and disagreed with the review's 8 — the difference was entirely the pattern, and the review's figure is the right one. Recording all three so nobody re-opens the question, which has already cost this project time on #250 where three counts disagreed until the criterion was fixed.

## Why it is worth a sweep rather than leaving

- It is a **reader-facing dead pointer** in published material, in the same class the contract already bans. A reader who goes looking for "the build note" finds nothing in the repository.
- It is **pre-existing and spreading**: 8 of 41 published recipes, and recipe 42 added two more before its review caught them. Each new recipe inherits the phrasing by reading its neighbours.
- The guard that enforces section 6 matches `#NNN` and "the issue" only — tracked as **#225** — so this spelling passes every check, as the other unlisted spellings have (`(M3)` finding labels, brief rule numbers, "the pull request's own report").

## What to do

Two pieces, and they are independent:

1. **A sweep PR** over the 9 files, replacing each reference with the property it stands for. These are mostly justifications for a fixture or a design choice, and the honest replacement is the reason itself — which is what a future reader needs anyway and what the recipe should have said.
2. **Add the spelling to `CONTRIBUTING.md` section 6**, or better, restate the rule by its reason rather than by a list of spellings. The list has now been evaded four times by different phrasings, which is strong evidence that enumerating spellings is the wrong shape for this rule.

If #225's guard is widened at the same time, this becomes mechanically enforced rather than a recurring review finding.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The 9 files no longer refer to a build note; each states the property instead.
- [ ] `CONTRIBUTING.md` section 6 covers the class rather than only `#NNN` and "the issue" — by reason, not by a longer list.
- [ ] The published set is re-measured under a written criterion and the result recorded here.
- [ ] If a check lands (see #225), it is proved by mutation on a planted reference and on a legitimate in-tree citation such as `CONTRIBUTING.md` section 6 or `docs/glossary.md`, which must keep passing.

title: Foundation: plot_confusion_matrix takes one label list for both axes and hardcodes Gold/Predicted, so a gold-content-versus-action matrix cannot be labelled correctly
body:
`jev_cookbook.style.plot_confusion_matrix` takes **one** label sequence used for **both** axes and hardcodes the axis titles `"Gold"` and `"Predicted"`. A recipe whose matrix is not gold-label-versus-same-label — for example gold **content** against final **action** — cannot be labelled correctly through it, and the resulting figure will contradict the table printed beside it.

Found by the Opus review of PR #260 (recipe 42), which **decoded and read the committed PNG** rather than inferring from the call site: its x axis read "Predicted: clear / violates" where the columns are `allowed` / `held`.

## Verified

`src/jev_cookbook/style.py:578-620`:

- the signature is `plot_confusion_matrix(counts, labels=None, *, normalize, title, ax)` — a **single** `labels`;
- it sets `ax.set_xlabel("Predicted")` and `ax.set_ylabel("Gold")` unconditionally;
- and `ConfusionMatrix` itself (`evaluation.py:280-285`) carries one `labels: list[Any]`, documented as *"`matrix[i, j]` is the number of examples whose gold option is `labels[i]` and whose predicted option is `labels[j]`"* — so the shared-vocabulary assumption runs through the data type as well as the plotter.

**26 published recipes plot a confusion matrix**, and every one of them compares a label against the *same* vocabulary, so none has needed anything else. Recipe 42 is the first to want a matrix whose two axes are different quantities, and it is not an exotic case: a Level 4 recipe that composes a model judgement with a Python action will routinely want **gold content × final action**, which is exactly a review-branch recipe's most interesting table.

## Why it is worth closing rather than working around

The consequence is a **figure that disagrees with the cell it sits in**. That is a worse failure than a missing figure, because a committed PNG reads as evidence and nobody re-decodes it — this instance survived until a reviewer thought to look inside the image. There is no check that could catch it either: the axis text is pixels, and the labels passed to the helper are perfectly valid for the helper's own contract.

The workaround available today is to relabel after the call, restructure the figure, or plot something whose axes genuinely do match — all of which push presentation logic into recipes, which is what the shared style module exists to prevent.

## Suggested fix

Add optional `row_labels` and `col_labels` (defaulting to `labels` for every existing caller), and optional axis titles defaulting to `"Gold"` and `"Predicted"`. All 26 current call sites keep working unchanged, and a recipe with two different vocabularies can describe its own axes.

Worth deciding at the same time whether `ConfusionMatrix` should gain the same optionality, or whether a two-vocabulary table is better served by a separate type — the docstring's "gold option / predicted option" wording is load-bearing for the single-vocabulary case and should not quietly become false.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `plot_confusion_matrix` accepts distinct row and column labels and distinct axis titles, with all existing call sites unchanged and passing.
- [ ] A test plots a matrix whose axes are different vocabularies and asserts the rendered axis text, so the defect that occasioned this cannot recur silently.
- [ ] A decision is recorded on whether `ConfusionMatrix` changes, and its docstring remains true either way.
- [ ] The published set is re-rendered and confirmed byte-identical, or any change is explained — 26 recipes commit one of these figures and a plotter change must not move them.

title: Foundation: a Next-steps exercise's quoted numbers are structurally unpinnable, and four recipes have shipped one wrong
body:
A recipe's "Next steps" exercise typically tells a reader to change a parameter and watch specific numbers move. **Those numbers are structurally unpinnable**: they describe a counterfactual run that the notebook never performs, so they appear in no committed output and no test, and nothing can notice when they are wrong.

**Four recipes have now shipped one of these wrong**, which is the strongest evidence in this repository that a class needs a mechanism rather than more care.

Found by the Opus review of PR #254 (recipe 41), which named the figures concerned: `4`, `0.0909` and `0.9091` appear nowhere in that recipe's committed output or tests.

## The four instances

| recipe | what was wrong |
|---|---|
| 38 | direction stated backwards **and** the exercise inert — lowering the parameter from 0.75 to 0.10 left the threshold unchanged, so a reader following it saw nothing |
| 39 | a false justification resting on the same misunderstanding of what the selector does |
| 40 | direction corrected, **exercise still inert** — the suggested value left the branching set, the disagreement set, accuracy, requests and the review set all identical, because the confidences are bimodal and every threshold in a wide gap gives the same answer |
| 41 | direction corrected and the exercise genuinely moves something — but its three quoted numbers are pinned by nothing |

Every one was caught by a reviewer **running the exercise**. None was caught by any check, and none could have been: the standing numeral sweep requires a figure to appear in committed output, and these figures deliberately describe a run the notebook does not make.

## Why this is a mechanism gap and not an attentiveness gap

The house guidance already says a prose claim about a property of the committed data needs a test, and already says to verify a reader exercise by running it. Recipe 41's builder did verify by running — and still quoted three numbers that nothing pins, because **there is nowhere for them to live**. The notebook computes the frozen threshold, not the counterfactual one.

So the author is asked to make a checkable claim about a computation the recipe is not allowed to perform (performing it would change committed output and the recipe's own numbers).

## Options, with their costs

1. **Compute the counterfactual and print it.** Make the exercise's claim an actual committed output — a small table of parameter → threshold → the two or three quantities that move. Then the numeral sweep covers it and a reader can check it without running anything. Cost: more committed output, and a decision about how much of a sweep is worth printing. Recipe 40 already prints a threshold sweep, so the shape exists.
2. **Pin it in a test instead.** A test re-derives the counterfactual through the shared helpers and asserts the quoted numbers. Cost: the numbers live in two places, which is the duplication the objective-pin work (#244) has been trying to remove — though here the second place is a test rather than a hand-written label, which is the safer direction.
3. **Forbid quoting specific numbers in an exercise.** "Raise the floor and watch the review set shrink" is checkable by a reader and unpinnable-by-construction, because it asserts a direction rather than a value. Cheapest, and it loses the most: a reader cannot tell whether what they observe is what the author saw.
4. **Require the exercise to name a value the author verified moves something**, without quoting outcomes. A middle point: it fixes the inert-exercise failure (recipes 38 and 40) without the pinning problem, and leaves the direction claim checkable.

Options 1 and 2 are mechanically checkable; 3 and 4 are conventions.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A decision is recorded with its reason, covering both failure modes this class has produced: a **wrong direction**, and an exercise that **demonstrates nothing**.
- [ ] If numbers may be quoted, there is a mechanism that notices when they are wrong, proved by mutation.
- [ ] If they may not, the guidance says what an exercise should say instead, with a worked example from the published set.
- [ ] The published set's existing exercises are checked under whatever lands, and the result recorded here.
- [ ] The relationship to #245 is stated — that issue covers the `min_coverage` direction specifically; this one is about the exercise's quoted outcomes whatever the parameter.

title: Foundation: no convention for a recipe whose coverage is mostly deterministic, where the metric describes the Python guard rather than the decision
body:
There is no house convention for a recipe whose **coverage numerator is mostly deterministic** — where most of the rows counted as "answered and correct" were decided by Python before the model's answer mattered. Recipe 41 is the first instance, and every upcoming permission, budget and interlock recipe will have the same shape.

Raised by the Opus review of PR #254, which found it while checking that recipe's baselines.

## The shape

Recipe 41 denies an action outright when a Python-checked approval binding fails, and only consults the model when the binding holds. Its reviewer measured the consequence: **7 of the mechanism's 10 answered rows are correct-by-construction denials** — correct because `check_binding` says so, not because any answer was good. It further established that the comparison baselines are **structurally determined**: `always_review`'s accuracy 1.0000 and risk 0.0000 are unchanged across **200 random gold assignments**, and `permission_only`'s coverage 1.0000 likewise.

So a headline coverage/accuracy/risk triple can look like a result about the decision while most of it is arithmetic about the deterministic guard. Nothing is false — the numbers are what they are — but a reader cannot tell from them what the model contributed.

## Why this needs a convention rather than a per-recipe fix

The family is large and immediately upcoming: permission checks, retry and spend budgets, approval bindings, stop conditions, interlocks. All of them are recipes where **Python decides most rows and the model decides the interesting remainder**, and all of them will report a metric dominated by the deterministic part. Each builder will face the same question with no guidance and will answer it differently.

The honest answer for recipe 41 turned out to be in its own data, and it points at the general form: report what the model's answers **changed**. That reviewer found it — **3 auto-executions that the always-review baseline would not make** (2 right, 1 wrong), and **wrong auto-executions cut from 5 to 1** against the permission-only baseline. Those are decision-level differences, and they are informative precisely where the aggregate triple is not.

This is also the fourth distinct way a metric has failed to support a recipe's lesson in this project — alongside saturation, blindness to inadequacy, and being matched more cheaply (all now in the house brief as rule 17 and rule 19). **Deterministic dominance is the fourth, and it deserves naming beside them.**

## What to decide

1. **Require the split.** When a recipe's rule has a deterministic branch, report the metric over the rows the model actually decided, alongside the whole-set figure — and say which is which. Cheap, and it makes the model's contribution visible without discarding the composed number.
2. **Require a decision-level comparison** against each baseline: not "accuracy differs by X" but "these N rows are decided differently, of which M are right". That is what a reader of an approval-gating recipe actually wants.
3. **Require disclosure of structural figures.** A baseline whose accuracy cannot move should say so — "1.0000 by construction, unchanged over 200 random gold assignments" is a far more useful sentence than "1.0000", and the test for it is cheap.

Any of these could be house guidance; 1 and 3 are mechanically checkable, 2 is not.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A convention is recorded in the reviewer and builder guidance, covering at least: when a deterministic branch dominates, what must be reported alongside the aggregate.
- [ ] A decision is recorded on whether any part of it is mechanically checked, and if so it is proved by mutation.
- [ ] Recipe 41 is cited as the worked example, and the family (permissions, budgets, interlocks) named so the next builder recognises itself.
- [ ] The relationship to rule 17 and rule 19 is stated, so the four failure modes sit together rather than being rediscovered separately.

title: Foundation: docs/notebook-style.md mandates the em dash in prose; 32 of 40 published notebooks use ASCII ' -- ' and no check enforces either
body:
`docs/notebook-style.md` mandates the Unicode em dash in markdown prose and the ASCII double-hyphen in code. The published set has drifted the other way in prose, and **no check enforces it**.

Raised by the Opus review of PR #254 as set-wide drift, explicitly not that recipe's to resolve. I measured it independently before filing.

## What the rule says

`docs/notebook-style.md:23-27`:
