> **Dashes.** A notebook's markdown cells and this cookbook's own docs use the Unicode em dash, `—`, for a parenthetical or appositive aside in prose. Code — comments, docstrings, shell snippets inside a fenced block — uses the ASCII double-hyphen, ` -- `, instead… in prose, use `—`.

So the division is by **context**: prose gets `—`, code gets ` -- `.

## What the set does

Measured over all 40 published recipes at `06cc0d7`, counting only **markdown** cells:

| | notebooks |
|---|---|
| contain ` -- ` in markdown prose | **32 of 40** |
| contain `—` in markdown prose | 9 of 40 |
| contain both | 2 |
| contain neither | 1 |

So the documented convention is the **minority** practice in the artefact it governs, and the ASCII form — which the rule assigns to code — is what most prose uses. (The reviewer reported 30 of 40; my 32 differs slightly by what counts as a dash context, and the conclusion is the same either way. Whoever acts on this should re-measure under a criterion they have written down, as happened on #250 where three counts disagreed until the criterion was fixed.)

There is **no guard** anywhere in `tests/` or `tools/` that looks at dashes.

## Why it is worth deciding rather than ignoring

- It is a **documented** rule with near-total non-compliance, which is the worst of both states: readers of the style doc are misled about the house convention, and a builder who follows the doc produces prose that looks inconsistent with 32 of its 40 neighbours.
- The fix direction is genuinely open. **Changing 32 notebooks** is a large sweep touching committed prose in every one, with the re-execution and invariance protocol that implies — for a purely typographic gain. **Changing the doc** to match practice is one edit, but gives up a real typographic distinction the doc argues for, and the em dash is the better form in rendered markdown.
- A middle option exists: keep the rule, enforce it **for new recipes only**, and record the existing set as grandfathered. That is honest and cheap, but this repository has found that unenforced-for-some rules decay (see #249 on skips keyed to the wrong property), so it needs a check that knows which recipes it applies to.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A decision is recorded with its reason: sweep the set, relax the doc, or grandfather with a scoped check.
- [ ] The criterion for "a dash in prose" is written down **before** counting, and the set re-measured under it.
- [ ] If a check lands, it distinguishes markdown prose from code cells, fenced blocks and inline code spans — the rule's own division — and is proved by mutation in both directions.
- [ ] If the doc is relaxed, `docs/notebook-style.md` says what the convention now is, so the next builder is not left inferring it from neighbours.

title: Foundation: no check requires a recipe to have any figure, so a figureless notebook satisfies both plot guards by vacuity
body:
Nothing checks that a recipe's notebook contains **any** figure. A figureless recipe therefore passes `figure_titles_check_only` and `print_what_you_plot` **by vacuity** — both iterate over plotting cells, and a notebook with none satisfies them trivially.

Found by the Opus review of PR #254 (recipe 41), which was the first notebook in the set with zero images.

## Measured

At `06cc0d7` (40 published), recipe 41's branch has **0 committed `image/png` outputs and 0 `plot_*` call sites** across 44 cells. Every other published recipe has at least one figure. So the norm is universal in practice and **mechanically unenforced**.

That reviewer ruled figureless **permissible in principle** — no rule requires a chart — but **not acceptable for that recipe**, on grounds worth preserving as the precedent:

- it was the only one of 40 notebooks with no images;
- it **emptied two guards by vacuity**, so a green run meant materially less than it appeared to;
- and its `min_coverage` sweep and three-way (coverage, risk) frontier are **exactly** the shapes `plot_threshold_sweep` and `plot_risk_coverage` exist for — the latter carrying its most contestable claim.

So the defect is not "no chart" in the abstract; it is a recipe whose data is chart-shaped presenting it as a table while two checks that exist to police figures report success.

## This is the same family as #249

That issue is about three guards skipping for a scripted recipe, and its argument applies here unchanged: **a check whose scope is "the plotting cells" silently becomes a check over the empty set.** A skip that is explicit at least appears as `s` in pytest output; vacuous satisfaction appears as a **pass**, which is worse.

## What to do

Add a guard requiring **at least one committed `image/png`** in every published recipe's notebook. It is one line of logic, needs no execution, and keys on the property rather than an idiom — the shape this repository has repeatedly found to be the durable kind (contrast #222, #227, #234, #244).

Decide and record one thing: whether it should be a hard failure or carry the **named-exemption** mechanism that already exists elsewhere in the guard module. A recipe genuinely better served by tables alone is imaginable; what is not acceptable is that case being indistinguishable from an oversight.

Note the companion rule when a figure is added: a plot reaches the notebook only as the **cell result**, so prints must come *before* the `plot_*` call, and the count must be taken **per cell**. A recipe lost a figure to a trailing `print` with every check green, which is why `print_what_you_plot` exists — and why a guard that only runs when figures already exist is the wrong shape.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A guard fails a published recipe whose notebook commits no `image/png`, proved by mutation on a recipe that currently passes.
- [ ] The published set passes it, or any exception is recorded here with its reason.
- [ ] A decision is recorded on hard-fail versus named exemption.
- [ ] The guard's docstring states that `figure_titles_check_only` and `print_what_you_plot` are vacuous without it, so the relationship is not left to be rediscovered.

title: Foundation: no check notices a number written as a WORD in recipe prose, which is how the one false count in a thrice-reviewed recipe survived
body:
Nothing in `tools/` or `tests/` notices a **number written as a word** in recipe prose. Every numeral check in this repository matches digits, so a false quantity spelled "nine" or "eight" is invisible to all of them — including the standing rule that every bare metric value in a markdown cell must appear in some code cell's committed output.

Raised by the Opus review of PR #253 (recipe 40) as a tooling idea it **could not settle**, which is why this issue is framed as a decision rather than a fix.

## The instance

Recipe 40's `evaluation-note-md` claimed "three real departments and at most three topics each — **nine leaves in total**". The committed taxonomy is **3/3/2**, so the real leaf count is **8**; the figure 9 is the *flat option list* (8 full paths **plus** the fallback), a different quantity. The recipe's own test and its own `helpers.py` comment already said 8+1.

It survived:

- a numeral sweep over the notebook (the word "nine" contains no digits);
- two full review rounds by a reviewer that caught four other defects in the same cell's neighbourhood;
- and the review that eventually found it reported *"because 'nine' is a word, no numeral sweep could ever flag it"*, and that it ran **no** numeral sweep in the final round for exactly that reason.

So this is not a hypothetical blind spot. It is the mechanism by which the single surviving false number in a heavily-reviewed recipe stayed invisible.

## Why it is a decision and not an obvious fix

A check for `one|two|…|twenty|dozen` in recipe markdown would be **noisy**. Number-words appear legitimately and often:

- ordinary prose that is not a quantity claim — "one of the two stages", "a second request", "either one";
- counts that are genuinely stable and not metrics — "the three real departments" is true and pinned;
- idiom — "one-to-one", "second-guess", "at one point".

So the plausible forms differ in cost:

1. **Flag every number-word in recipe markdown.** Cheapest to write, noisiest; would need a per-recipe allowlist, which is the mechanism this repository has repeatedly found decays (see #249 on skips keyed to the wrong property).
2. **Flag a number-word only when it modifies a counting noun** — "nine leaves", "three departments", "eight paths" — a small pattern over `number-word + plural noun`. Narrower, still noisy, but the noise is concentrated on exactly the sentences that *are* quantity claims, which is arguably the right place for a reviewer's attention.
3. **Require that a quantity claim be pinned rather than detected**, which is the direction the rest of this repository has gone: a prose claim about a property of the committed structure needs a test, whatever spelling it uses. That does not need a lint at all — it needs the house rule, which already exists — and it is what actually fixed recipe 40 (a new test pinning `{3,3,2}` → 8 → 9, with each half of `8 + 1` provably pinned separately).

Option 3 is the only one that addresses the cause rather than the spelling, and it is already house guidance — so **the honest question this issue asks is whether a lint adds anything on top of it, or whether the right outcome is to record that the numeral sweep is structurally blind to number-words and rely on pinning.**

Recording the latter would be a legitimate resolution, provided it is written where builders and reviewers will read it rather than left implicit.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A decision is recorded, with its reason — lint (which form), or no lint plus an explicit note of the blind spot.
- [ ] If a lint lands: proved by mutation on recipe 40's original wording, and measured against the whole published set for its false-positive rate **before** adoption, with the rate recorded here.
- [ ] If no lint lands: the numeral sweep's blindness to number-words is stated in the reviewer and builder guidance, next to the sweep instruction itself rather than elsewhere.
- [ ] Either way, the stronger rule is stated: **a prose claim about a property of the committed structure needs a test, whatever spelling the number uses.**

title: Foundation: the inbound-link audit accepts a link in ANY markdown cell, while the rule it implements is about the Next steps section
body:
`test_every_recipe_is_linked_from_some_other_recipes_next_steps` is named for the **Next steps** section but accepts a link in **any markdown cell** of any published recipe. So a future wave close-out could turn the audit green with a target mentioned only in passing mid-notebook, and the check would report full inbound coverage that no reader would experience as a next step.

Found by the Opus review of PR #251, the Wave 3 close-out sweep. **Not triggered there** — that reviewer confirmed all eleven of the sweep's new links are in `next-md` cells — so this is a latent gap, not a backlog.

## The mechanism

`_inbound_next_steps_links` (`tests/test_recipe_guard.py:872-884`) iterates every cell, skips non-markdown, and records any `](../NN-slug/)` match:

```python
for cell in notebook_cells(recipe_dir(recipe)):
    if cell["cell_type"] != "markdown":
        continue
    for slug in NEIGHBOUR_LINK.findall(cell_source(cell)):
        ...
```

There is no restriction to the Next steps cell, and none to its position.

The rule it implements is narrower. `CONTRIBUTING.md:91`: *"**Close** with what to try next and links to neighbouring recipes. A **'Next steps'** link names a neighbour that already exists on `main`"*. The rule is about a section at the end of the notebook; the check is about a string anywhere in it.

## Why it is worth closing rather than leaving

- **The audit is the only enforcement of this rule**, and it runs by hand at a wave close-out. If it can be satisfied incidentally, then the one moment anyone checks inbound coverage is the moment it can be satisfied without the reader-facing property existing.
- **Incidental links are not rare.** Recipes legitimately link to neighbours mid-notebook when discussing a shared pattern — the sibling check `next_steps_links_exist` exists partly because they do. So the loose form is not a theoretical hole; it is one an ordinary recipe could close by accident, which also means a genuine gap could be **masked** by an unrelated mention.
- It is the same shape as several findings already tracked here: a check keyed on something adjacent to the property rather than the property itself. See #222, #227, #234, #244, #249.

## The decision to make

Either narrow the check or soften the rule — both are defensible and the issue should record which was chosen and why:

1. **Narrow the check**: locate the Next steps cell and scan only it. The cells are conventionally identified (`next-md` across the published set), but keying on a cell id would be brittle and is itself the subject of #250; keying on the heading text (`## Next steps`) is more robust and matches what a reader sees.
2. **Soften the rule**: decide that any inbound link anywhere counts, and reword `CONTRIBUTING.md:91` so the contract matches the check. Cheaper, and arguably fine — a reader who meets a link mid-notebook does follow it — but it gives up the "close with what to try next" structure the rule currently asks for.

Option 1 is the better fit for why the rule exists, but it has a real cost: it would **fail** any recipe whose only inbound link is incidental, so whichever is chosen, **audit the published set under the new rule before landing it** and report the delta here.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A decision is recorded, with its reason.
- [ ] If the check is narrowed: the published set is audited under the new form first, and any recipe failing only because its inbound link is incidental is fixed in the same pass or recorded here.
- [ ] If the rule is softened: `CONTRIBUTING.md:91` is reworded so the contract and the check agree.
- [ ] Either way, the check's docstring states which it is, so the next reader of the audit does not have to derive it.
- [ ] Proved by mutation: a planted mid-notebook-only link either does or does not satisfy the audit, matching whichever decision was taken.

title: Foundation: recipes cite their own cell ids in reader-facing prose, and a cell id is invisible in the rendered notebook
body:
Recipe notebooks cite their own **cell ids** in reader-facing prose — "the `python-rule` cell below", "as `evaluation-curve` shows". A cell id exists only in the `.ipynb` JSON. **A reader of the rendered notebook — in Jupyter, in nbviewer, on GitHub — never sees it.** So the pointer resolves to nothing for the audience it was written for.

Found by the Opus review of PR #242 as a set-wide convention problem rather than that recipe's invention.

This is the same class as `CONTRIBUTING.md` section 6's ban on citing issue numbers and "the issue" — *"a reader cannot see either"* — and the rule's stated reason governs this spelling too, even though its illustrative list does not mention cell ids. It is also a near-relative of the evidence-pointer trap already in the house rules: a claim that cites its own evidence location must be checkable **from where it points**, and here the pointer is invisible at the destination.

## Two counts, from two different criteria — neither is authoritative yet

**The reviewer reports 13 instances across 9 recipes**: 07, 17×2, 18, 19, 21, 22×2, 28×4, 32×2, 39×2.

**My own scan finds 9 across 5** — backticked tokens in markdown cells or `README.md` that exactly match a cell id of the same recipe, measured on `main` at `0c1f2bf`:

| recipe | citations |
|---|---|
| `14-source-span-selection` | `state` |
| `17-passage-reranking` | `selective-discuss`, `python-rule` |
| `19-ci-failure-classification` | `eval-validation-discuss` |
| `28-skill-selection` | `python-md`, `python-rule`, `evaluation-curve` |
| `32-regression-test-selection` | `counterfactual-code`, `python-rule` |

The sets overlap but differ in both directions — I find recipe 14, the reviewer finds 07, 18, 21 and 22; two of its 13 are in recipe 39, which is not yet on `main` and so is outside my scan. The likely cause is different criteria: whether an unbackticked mention counts, whether a citation inside a code comment counts (invisible to a reader in a different way, and arguably fine), and whether an id that is also an ordinary English word (`state`, `setup`) counts when the surrounding sentence may not be pointing at the cell at all.

**So establishing the real set is part of the work, not a precondition for it** — and the criterion needs deciding before counting, which is exactly where my count and the reviewer's diverged. Recording both rather than picking one, because a number that disagrees with another measurement and is not reconciled is how a figure goes stale in this repository.

## What a fix looks like

Cells are already referred to in two reader-visible ways elsewhere in the set, and either works: **quote the section heading** the cell sits under, or **describe the cell by what it prints** ("the sweep below", "the cell that prints the confusion matrix"). Both survive rendering and both survive a cell being renamed, which a cell-id citation does not.

Note the one legitimate use to preserve: **tests** that locate a cell by id (`next(c for c in cells if c.get("id") == "python-rule")`) are correct and must not be swept — that is machinery reading JSON, not prose addressed to a reader. Several recipes' objective pins depend on exactly that, so a careless fix would break them.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A criterion for "cites a cell id in reader-facing prose" is decided and written down, distinguishing markdown prose and README text (in scope) from code comments and test lookups (out of scope).
- [ ] The published set is counted under that criterion and the result recorded here, reconciling the two counts above.
- [ ] Each instance is rewritten to a reader-visible reference (heading, or what the cell prints).
- [ ] A check keys on the property — a backticked token in a markdown cell or README that matches a cell id of that notebook — and is proved by mutation to fire on a planted instance and not on a test's id lookup.
- [ ] `CONTRIBUTING.md` section 6 names this spelling, so the rule's reason is not left to be rediscovered a third time.

title: Foundation: three recipe-guard checks skip for a scripted recipe, one of which would FAIL — and the skips are keyed on responses.json rather than on the property each check means
body:
Recipe 36 (#246) will be the **first scripted recipe published** — one with no `fixtures/responses.json`. Three recipe-guard checks **skip** for such a recipe rather than run, and `tests/test_recipe_guard.py`'s own module docstring still says *"a scripted recipe; none are published yet"*, which goes stale the moment it merges. A green guard run therefore means materially less on a scripted recipe than on any other, and it reads exactly like a pass.

Found while reviewing PR #246, which verified each skipped check **by hand** and reported what it substituted — so this issue carries measurements, not predictions.

## The three skips, and what the review established about each

| check | line | status when verified by hand |
|---|---|---|
| `build_fixtures_scaffold` byte-identity | 270 | **Skip is correct.** Genuinely vacuous: there is no `build_fixtures.py`-generated `test_build_fixtures.py` to hold byte-identical. |
| `readme_budget_note_matches_stored_answers` | 1044 | **Would PASS.** The reviewer instrumented `decide` and measured **290** calls, matching the README including its per-cell breakdown. So the check is skipped on a recipe that satisfies it — a lost confirmation rather than a hidden defect, but lost silently. |
| **strong-form `G1(c)` threshold guard** | 463 | **Would FAIL.** With the skip removed, 36 recipes pass and recipe 36 alone fails. The cause was a test **name** rather than its shape (tracked separately as the anchor problem), but the point stands: the skip concealed a real guard failure. |

That third row is the one that matters. The skip is keyed on the wrong thing: `G1(c)` is about whether a recipe that **freezes a confidence threshold** re-derives it independently, and that property has nothing to do with whether the recipe's answers were stored or scripted. Recipe 36 **does** freeze a confidence gate — so the check was applicable, skipped, and would have failed.

## Suggested fix, per check

1. **`G1(c)` (line 463): key the skip on whether the recipe has a confidence gate, not on whether `responses.json` exists.** That is the property the check is about. A scripted recipe with a gate should be checked; a recipe without a gate should be skipped whatever its fixtures look like.
2. **`readme_budget_note_matches_stored_answers` (line 1044): derive the count from the notebook's actual `decide` calls** rather than from `len(responses.json)`, which would make it applicable to scripted recipes and simultaneously close the much more serious gap tracked in #213 (a doubly-decided example is invisible in a dict keyed by request state). The reviewer's hand-instrumentation is the working prototype.
3. **`build_fixtures_scaffold` (line 270): leave the skip.** It is genuinely vacuous and a skip is the honest outcome.
4. **Update the module docstring**, which will be false on merge, and say in it which checks do not apply to a scripted recipe and why — so the next reviewer of a scripted recipe starts from the list rather than deriving it.

## The general point, which is worth more than the three fixes

**A skipped check is the quietest kind of gap.** It produces a green run, contributes a line of `s` to pytest output nobody reads, and is indistinguishable from coverage unless someone goes looking. Two of these three skips were keyed on a proxy (`responses.json` exists) for a property they actually care about (does this recipe store answers / does it freeze a gate / does it make live requests), which is the same pattern already tracked in #222, #227, #234 and #244 — a check keyed on an idiom standing in for the thing it means.

It would be worth a standing rule that **a skip condition must name the property, not a correlate of it**, and that any new skip is accompanied by a test proving the check does something on a recipe where it *does* apply.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `G1(c)` runs on a scripted recipe that freezes a confidence gate, proved by mutation on recipe 36.
- [ ] The README live-call check applies to scripted recipes, or a recorded decision explains why it cannot.
- [ ] The module docstring is true after recipe 36 merges and enumerates the scripted-recipe skips with reasons.
- [ ] The published set is re-run with each skip condition temporarily removed, and any newly-failing recipe recorded here.

title: Foundation: notebook discovery re-executes an unrelated published recipe when pull_request.base.sha goes stale
body:
On a pull request whose `pull_request.base.sha` has gone stale, the notebook discovery job selects and **re-executes an unrelated, already-published recipe's notebook**. No correctness impact — wasted CI minutes and a confusing extra check row that reads as though the branch touched a recipe it does not contain.

Found incidentally during the review of PR #241, which chased it to a complete explanation rather than leaving it as a curiosity.

## The mechanism, established rather than guessed

1. `actions/checkout` on a `pull_request` event checks out the **merge ref**, so recently-merged recipes are present on disk.
2. `pull_request.base.sha` is pinned to `main`'s tip **at the time the PR opened**, not its current tip. For PR #241 that was `0ad22602` while `main` had since gained `d23a7f68` ("Recipe 37 (#236)").
3. The discovery job's **three-dot diff** against that stale base therefore reports `recipes/37-research-domain-tagging/` as changed.
4. `select()` keeps it, because the merge checkout genuinely has that notebook on disk.

Result: PR #241 carried a `Notebook (37-research-domain-tagging)` check alongside its own `Notebook (38-abstention-and-review-queues)`, and executed recipe 37's notebook in full.

The reviewer confirmed the branch is innocent two ways: the branch's tree contains **no `recipes/37-*` at all**, and it rebuilt the merge tree locally as a dangling commit and **reproduced CI's job matrix byte-for-byte**. So this is entirely a property of which base the diff is taken against.

## Why it is worth a small fix

- **It scales with merge rate.** Every recipe that merges while another PR is open adds one spurious notebook execution to that PR, on every subsequent push. With a 60-recipe cookbook and several PRs open at once, that is a steady multiplier on the slowest job in CI.
- **It makes a check row mean the wrong thing.** A reviewer seeing `Notebook (<other recipe>)` on a branch has to establish from scratch that the branch did not touch that recipe — which cost this review real time, and would cost every reviewer the same until it is documented or fixed.
- **It is adjacent to a readiness rule.** The merge-readiness helper judges each named check on its own, and a spurious check name appearing and disappearing between heads is exactly the kind of instability that rule exists to be strict about. It happens to be benign here because the job passes.

## Suggested fix

Diff against the **merge commit's own first parent** rather than `pull_request.base.sha` — on a merge-ref checkout, `HEAD^1` is the true current base, so the diff reports only what the branch actually changes. The reviewer proposed exactly this, and the reproduction above is evidence it would have produced the right matrix.

A cheaper alternative, if the workflow should stay simple: intersect the discovered set with the paths `tools/check_recipe_scope.py` already considers in scope for the PR, so a recipe folder the branch cannot legally have touched is never selected.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A pull request opened before an unrelated recipe merges does **not** acquire a `Notebook (<that recipe>)` check on its next push.
- [ ] The branch's own notebook is still discovered and executed in every case it is today — proved by a case where the recipe genuinely is modified.
- [ ] Whatever lands is reproducible the way this was diagnosed: rebuild the merge tree and confirm the job matrix matches what CI selects.

title: Foundation: a Noul confidence gate at or below |2t-1| can never block an accept, and docs/evaluation.md never names the case
body:
`docs/evaluation.md` describes the three-path pattern (accept / review / reject) and warns that a Noul's confidence is **distance from 0.5**, not margin at the business threshold — but it stops short of the consequence, which is that **a confidence gate at or below `|2t − 1|` can never block an accept.** A recipe can therefore ship a confidence gate that is mathematically incapable of changing any outcome, with every check green and a by-reason table implying a role the gate did not earn.

Found by the Opus review of PR #242 (recipe 39), which measured it rather than inferring it.

## The mathematics

For a Noul, `confidence = |2·noul − 1|`. An answer is accepted when `noul >= t` for a business threshold `t > 0.5`. Then:

```
noul >= t  >  0.5   ⟹   2·noul − 1 >= 2t − 1 > 0   ⟹   confidence >= 2t − 1 = |2t − 1|
```

So **every accepted answer already has confidence at least `|2t − 1|`**. A gate set at or below that value is satisfied by construction for everything the business threshold admits. It cannot defer a single accept; it can only choose the *reason* attached to answers the threshold already rejected.

## The instance

Recipe 39 froze `t = 0.85` and a gate of `0.70`, and `|2(0.85) − 1| = 0.70` **exactly** — the degenerate boundary, hit precisely rather than approached. Measured consequences:

- A sweep of 1001 noul values: **0 outcome differences**, 699 reason-only differences.
- **Removing the gate entirely** leaves `test` at an identical `0.9286 / 0.9615 / 0.0385`.

Both numbers were produced by the reviewer, and the second is the decisive one: a branch whose deletion changes no reported metric is not doing the work the notebook says it does.

## Why this is a documentation gap rather than only a recipe defect

- **The two thresholds are selected by different helpers against different quantities**, so a builder picking a plausible `t` and a plausible gate has no reason to notice they have collided. Nothing in the API or the docs connects them.
- **It is not a near-miss condition.** The failure is an inequality over a whole region, not a coincidence at one value: *any* gate `<= |2t − 1|` is degenerate. A builder who picks `t = 0.9` and a gate of `0.75` has the same dead branch and the same misleading by-reason table.
- **Every Noul three-path recipe can land here**, and the symptom is invisible: the notebook runs, the metrics are real, the table has rows. Only a counterfactual — delete the branch and see whether anything moves — exposes it, and nothing currently asks for one.
- This repository has already paid for the adjacent defect twice: a gate selected against a correctness criterion that was constant across thresholds, and a "diagnostic" gate whose function was never called, where deleting 2,414 characters left the notebook byte-identical.

## What to do

1. **State the consequence in `docs/evaluation.md`**, beside the existing distance-from-0.5 warning: for a Noul, a confidence gate must **exceed `|2t − 1|`** to be capable of deferring an accept, and give the derivation above so a reader can check it.
2. **Add a mechanical check**: for a recipe that freezes both a Noul business threshold and a confidence gate, fail when `gate <= |2t − 1|`. This is exactly computable from two committed constants, needs no execution, and is the rare case where a guard can test the property rather than an idiom standing in for it.
3. Consider requiring, for any confidence gate, a **printed counterfactual** showing what changes when the branch is removed. That generalises beyond this degeneracy to every dead branch, and it is the check that would have caught both prior instances as well as this one.
4. Audit the published Noul three-path recipes for `gate <= |2t − 1|` and record the result here.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `docs/evaluation.md` states the `|2t − 1|` floor with its derivation.
- [ ] A check fails closed when a frozen gate cannot block an accept, proved by mutation on a recipe whose gate is currently valid.
- [ ] The published set is audited and the per-recipe result recorded here.
- [ ] A decision is recorded on item 3 — implemented, or rejected with a reason.

title: Foundation: docs/evaluation.md does not document how min_coverage moves the frozen threshold (direction is inverse, and flat over a wide range)
body:
`docs/evaluation.md` documents `target_accuracy`'s selection behaviour at length and says **nothing** about how the frozen threshold responds when `min_coverage` moves. The direction is counter-intuitive, and recipe 38's builder got it backwards in shipped prose — stating it in a "Next steps" exercise it invited readers to run.

Found by the Opus review of PR #241.

## The behaviour, measured

**Raising `min_coverage` pushes the frozen threshold DOWN**, because a higher coverage floor forces the selector to admit more answers, which means accepting lower-confidence ones. So the relationship between the parameter and the threshold is *inverse*, while the relationship between the parameter and coverage is direct.

The reviewer established it on a 3-point pool through the real `select_confidence_threshold`:

- `min_coverage=0.6` → threshold `0.7`
- `min_coverage=0.3` → threshold `0.9`

And on recipe 38's own pool the behaviour has a flat region that makes the direction even easier to get wrong: lowering `min_coverage` from 0.75 all the way to **0.10** leaves the threshold unchanged at `0.7067`, and only raising it to 0.80+ moves it, to `0.1200`. A builder experimenting downward from the default would see **nothing happen** and could reasonably conclude the parameter barely matters.

## Why this is worth documenting rather than leaving to discovery

- **A builder already got it backwards in shipped prose**, and wrote a reader exercise around the wrong direction. The prose contained **no numeral**, so the standing numeral-versus-output sweep was blind to it; only a reviewer deriving the behaviour caught it.
- The two parameters read as symmetric alternatives in the API, and `docs/evaluation.md` reinforces that by describing one carefully and the other barely. A reader's natural inference — that `min_coverage` relates to the threshold the way `target_accuracy` does — is wrong.
- The **flat region** is the part no amount of care substitutes for documentation: a parameter that provably does nothing across a wide range, then moves the threshold sharply, is exactly the shape that teaches a wrong lesson to anyone who probes it casually.

## What to do

- Document `min_coverage`'s direction explicitly in `docs/evaluation.md`, beside the existing `target_accuracy` material, stating that raising the coverage floor lowers the threshold.
- Note that the response can be **flat over a wide range of the parameter** for a given pool, with recipe 38's pool as the worked example if a concrete one helps.
- Say plainly what the two objectives are for, since this is the second recipe to reach for one and argue for it on grounds that do not hold: `target_accuracy` constrains the accuracy of the **answered subset**, which is a different denominator from whole-split per-question accuracy, and the two are easy to confuse because both are called accuracy. That confusion is itself the substance of one of recipe 38's must-changes.
- Add the 3-point counterexample above (or an equivalent) as a test beside the helper, so the documented direction cannot silently drift from the implementation.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `docs/evaluation.md` states `min_coverage`'s direction and notes the possible flat region.
- [ ] The answered-subset-versus-whole-split distinction is stated where a reader choosing between the two objectives will see it.
- [ ] A test pins the documented direction, so prose and implementation cannot diverge.

title: Foundation: nothing pins a notebook's threshold OBJECTIVE — a keyword swap ships a byte-identical notebook with a false printed objective line, all checks green
body:
Nothing mechanical pins a notebook's threshold **objective**. A recipe can swap `min_coverage=0.75` for `target_accuracy=1.0`, leave its hand-written printed `objective:` line untouched, and ship a **byte-identical notebook whose printed objective line is false** — with the full suite, the recipe guard and the notebook freshness check all green.

Found by the Opus review of PR #241 (recipe 38), which demonstrated it three ways rather than arguing it.

## The three mutations, all green

On recipe 38 at `ab235252fe511237bf7f3660dfc56cb5e3710d0f`:

1. **Change the objective's value and re-execute.** `min_coverage` 0.75 → 0.85 freezes a different threshold (`0.7067` → `0.1200`), moves coverage `0.6500` → `0.7500`, moves risk `0.0769` → `0.0667`, and flips a demo ticket's outcome. **All 524 tests pass.**
2. **Swap the keyword, keep the printed literal.** `min_coverage=0.75` → `target_accuracy=1.0` while the hand-written `objective:` f-string stays as it was. On this pool both objectives return the same threshold, so the notebook is **byte-identical** — and its printed claim about which objective ran is now false. **Suite, guard and freshness all green.**
3. **Change the pinned value in the test.** Replacing `0.75` with 0.60, 0.85 or 0.95 in `tests/` is **also inert**.

The only mutation that gets caught is an edit the author does **not** re-execute, caught by freshness — which is precisely the case a careful builder never produces.

## Why the usual pin does not work

Two things that look like pins are not:

- **A printed f-string literal** (`print(f"objective: select_confidence_threshold(..., min_coverage=0.75)")`) is written by hand beside the call, and **nothing compares the two**. It is a decoration that happens to look like evidence, and it is worse than nothing because it reads as a trace to committed output.
- **A test asserting the resulting threshold value.** The value is a *consequence* of the objective, so pinning it constrains the objective only if no other objective can produce that value — which is exactly what has not been checked, and on this pool two objectives produce the same value.

This is the same family as several findings already tracked here: a check keyed on an idiom standing in for a property it cannot observe. See #222 for the strong-form guard, #227 for the reason-string guard, #234 for the validation-metric-line guard.

## What does work

Parse the **committed notebook cell source** and assert the objective's spelling appears in it — the route recipes 31, 32, 34 and 37 took. A keyword swap changes the cell source, so the assertion fails. Pair it with the value assertion: the spelling pins *which objective*, the value pins *which answer*, and neither alone is sufficient.

## Scope — likely set-wide, and deliberately not quantified here

A crude scan of the published set suggests only a minority of recipes assert the objective's **keyword** at all, and only a handful parse the notebook's own cell source. **I am not putting a number on it**, because the scan is an approximate regex over test files and multi-line assertions defeat it — the same class of approximation that has produced two wrong conclusions in this repository today. The audit has to be done by **mutation, per recipe**, which is the only instrument that has given a trustworthy answer so far.

What is established: recipe 38's pin is inert, demonstrated three ways; and the mechanism that makes it inert (a hand-written printed literal plus a value-only assertion) is not specific to that recipe.

## What to do

1. Add a guard that, for any recipe whose notebook selects a confidence threshold, requires the **objective keyword** as spelled in the committed cell source to be asserted somewhere in that recipe's `tests/`. Fail closed.
2. Audit the published set **by mutation**: for each recipe, swap the objective keyword, re-execute, and record whether anything goes red. Record the per-recipe result here.
3. Fix the drift found through the normal reviewed pipeline, not inside recipe pull requests open for other purposes.
4. Update `docs/recipe-template.md` and the template's own test so the working form is what new recipes inherit — the template is what every rule here is written to match, and a builder following it should get a real pin for free.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A keyword swap on any published recipe's threshold objective turns something red, proved by mutation on each.
- [ ] The guard fails closed and names the recipe and the expected spelling.
- [ ] The template ships a working pin, so the default is correct rather than optional.
- [ ] The per-recipe mutation audit is recorded here, including any recipe where the two objectives coincide on its pool (those are the ones where a value-only assertion is most misleading).

title: Foundation: check_hygiene rejects ordinary keyword arguments whose constant name contains a letter-digit run (STAGE1, SHA256)
body:
`tools/check_hygiene.py`'s high-entropy-token rule rejects ordinary Python keyword arguments whose value is a constant with a digit inside a word — `STAGE1`, `SHA256`, `UTF8`, `V2` — forcing an author to rename working code to satisfy a secret scanner. It cost recipe 39's builder a rename, and the builder treated it as its own problem rather than a repository one, so it would have gone unreported.

## Reproduced

Three probe files, run through the real scanner:

```
$ cat probe_bad.py
_STAGE1_INSTRUCTIONS = "Pick the span stating the invoice number."
q = build([omitted; sha256: 38d9efe42675fc8f1746f4234326b75fe3a5c8291b62753c26ca46a0dd8ad986])

$ python3 tools/check_hygiene.py probe_bad.py
probe_bad.py: line 2: [high-entropy-token] inst****** (len 33)
exit 1
```

```
$ cat probe_good.py            # identical but for one underscore
_STAGE_1_INSTRUCTIONS = "..."
q = build(instructions=_STAGE_1_INSTRUCTIONS)

$ python3 tools/check_hygiene.py probe_good.py
Hygiene check passed: 1 file(s) scanned.
exit 0
```

And it is not specific to `STAGE1`:

```
$ cat probe_sha.py
SHA256_DIGEST_PREFIX_NAME = "abc"
v = verify([omitted; sha256: e65345028ecd95063b190d5e61c19a40b1a03bf50b7d904ce397e089fccdc3c0])

$ python3 tools/check_hygiene.py probe_sha.py
probe_sha.py: line 2: [high-entropy-token] dige****** (len 39)
exit 1
```

## Mechanism

Two rules interact, and each is individually reasonable:

1. `_TOKEN = re.compile(r"[A-Za-z0-9_+=-]{32,}")` (line 162) **includes `=`**, so a whole `name=VALUE` keyword argument of 32 characters or more is scanned as **one token**. `[omitted; sha256: 38d9efe42675fc8f1746f4234326b75fe3a5c8291b62753c26ca46a0dd8ad986]` is exactly 33 characters.
2. `_IDENT_ASSIGNMENT` (line 178) is the exemption that says such a thing is code, not a secret — but as its own comment states, it requires that **"no run mixes letters with digits"**. `STAGE1` is one run mixing both, so the exemption does not match.

The token then reaches the entropy rule at line 207-208, where `mixed = any(c.isalpha()) and any(c.isdigit() or c in "+/=")` is true and the entropy of the full 33-character string clears the 4.2 threshold. Flagged.

So the trigger is: **a keyword argument whose combined `name=VALUE` length is ≥ 32 and whose identifier contains a letter-digit run.** Nothing about the code is unusual, and no value is present at all — the "token" is two identifiers and an equals sign.

## Why it is worth fixing rather than renaming around

- **The workaround is invisible.** An author hits it, renames, and moves on; nothing records that the scanner forced a naming decision. It was found here only because a builder mentioned the rename in passing, and it had already concluded there was no foundation gap to report.
- **The names it rejects are conventional.** `SHA256_`, `UTF8_`, `BASE64_`, `STAGE1_`, `V2_` are ordinary prefixes, and the digit-inside-a-word form is the usual spelling for all of them. `_STAGE_1_` is not better code; it is code shaped around a scanner.
- **It is a false positive in a check whose false negatives matter.** Every spurious rejection trains an author to treat this scanner as noise, which is the opposite of what a secret scanner needs. The scanner is otherwise good and has a real job — the repository's key lives outside every worktree and must never reach a commit.

## Suggested fix

Relax `_IDENT_ASSIGNMENT`'s run rule to allow a run that mixes letters and digits **provided it is not all-digits and not plausibly base64** — or, more simply, exempt a `name=VALUE` token where **both sides are valid Python identifiers** and the right side contains no quote, slash, plus or equals. A real secret assigned inline is a literal, not an identifier, so identifier-on-both-sides is a strong and cheap discriminator.

Whatever lands, add the three probes above as test cases, and **prove the rule still fails closed** by checking that a genuine high-entropy literal assigned to a plausibly-named constant is still caught.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `[omitted; sha256: 38d9efe42675fc8f1746f4234326b75fe3a5c8291b62753c26ca46a0dd8ad986]` and `[omitted; sha256: e65345028ecd95063b190d5e61c19a40b1a03bf50b7d904ce397e089fccdc3c0]` pass.
- [ ] A real high-entropy literal still fails, proved by mutation rather than asserted.
- [ ] The three probes above exist as regression tests.
- [ ] The published set is re-scanned under the new rule and the result recorded here; recipe 39's `_STAGE_1_INSTRUCTIONS` naming may then be left as-is or reverted, as its author prefers — it is not wrong, merely shaped around this.

title: Foundation: no top-k ranking-accuracy helper in jev_cookbook.evaluation (recipe 17 documents the gap in three committed files)
body:
`jev_cookbook.evaluation` has no helper for top-k ranking accuracy — "was the top-scored item in this ranked list relevant?" — and the absence has already caused one real defect and one near-identical trap.

Recipe 17 documents the gap **three times in committed files a reader can open**: `recipes/17-passage-reranking/helpers.py:178-195`, `README.md:91-92`, and the notebook's `ranking-md` cell. It asks explicitly for a foundation fix and was never filed. This issue is that filing.

## The gap

Neither existing helper answers the question:

- `mean_ndcg` averages `ndcg` over several ranked lists — a graded ranking quality measure, not a top-1 hit rate.
- `top_k_accuracy` is for a **single `Choice`-style probability distribution over one example's options**, not a ranked list of per-item scores across several queries.

## The defect it already caused

Recipe 17 originally computed `top1_accuracy` as the mean of `evaluation.recall_at_budget(relevant, scores, 1)` over queries, *"on the mistaken assumption that the two always agree"*. They do not. `recall_at_budget` reports the share of **all** relevant items a budget of 1 would reach, so it returns **0.5 for two relevant items among three even when the single top-scored item is itself relevant**.

The part worth preserving is how it survived: **that recipe's own fixtures hid it, because every query there has exactly one gold-`direct` passage** — and with one relevant item per query the two quantities coincide exactly. A uniform fixture set made a wrong metric look right.

That is the same shape as #231, where `recall_at_budget` credited candidates a confidence gate had excluded and produced `0.6667` where the rule's own pick gives `0.5`. Both are **the helper answering a neighbouring question to the one asked**, not the helper being buggy, and in both the fixture set was too uniform to reveal it. See #231 for the invariant that catches this class — a task-level metric must equal what the rule's own composition produces, checked on every committed example.

## What to do

Recipe 17 already has a working implementation and a test that pins the distinction, so this is closer to a move than a design:

- `helpers.top1_accuracy` (`recipes/17-passage-reranking/helpers.py:198`) computes it directly, using the same expectation-over-tie-orders convention `recall_at_budget` uses.
- `tests/test_helpers.py::test_top1_accuracy_differs_from_recall_at_a_budget_of_one` is the regression pin, and it is the test that makes the promotion safe — it fails if the two are ever conflated again.

Recipe 17's own instruction on the shape of the fix should be honoured: *"as its own helper, **not a wrapper around `recall_at_budget`**"*. A wrapper reintroduces the conflation at one remove.

Generalise to top-**k** rather than top-1 only if the signature stays honest about ties; top-1 is what any recipe needs today.

## Also worth doing while in there

Add a docstring note to `recall_at_budget` naming both traps it has now caused — that it credits ineligible candidates unless the budget is eligibility-aware (#231), and that it is not top-1 accuracy when a query has more than one relevant item — with a pointer to the new helper. Both defects cost a recipe a round, and both were discoverable only by someone already suspicious.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A top-k (or top-1) ranking-accuracy helper exists in `jev_cookbook.evaluation`, computed directly rather than via `recall_at_budget`, with the tie convention documented.
- [ ] Recipe 17's local `top1_accuracy` is replaced by the shared helper, or a recorded decision explains why it stays local.
- [ ] `test_top1_accuracy_differs_from_recall_at_a_budget_of_one`, or an equivalent, lives beside the new helper so the conflation cannot return.
- [ ] `recall_at_budget`'s docstring names both traps and points at the new helper.
- [ ] The published set is checked for any other use of `recall_at_budget` standing in for a top-k metric, and the result recorded here. (Audited at `6544111`: three recipes touch it — 32 uses it with an eligibility-aware budget, 15 uses it correctly over an ungated ranking and says so in prose, 17 does not call it at all. No further instances today.)

title: Foundation: DecisionResult has __getitem__ but no __contains__, so 'name in result' raises KeyError(0) via the legacy sequence protocol
body:
`DecisionResult` defines `__getitem__` but neither `__contains__` nor `__iter__`. I verified it directly:

```
has __contains__: False
has __iter__    : False
has __getitem__ : True
```

(`src/jev_cookbook/answers.py:458`.)

Python's `in` operator, absent `__contains__`, falls back to the **old iteration protocol**: it calls `__getitem__` with `0`, `1`, `2`, … until `IndexError`. `DecisionResult.__getitem__` is keyed by **question name**, so `0` is not a valid key and it raises **`KeyError(0)`** instead of returning a boolean or raising something a caller can read.

So this, which looks obviously correct:

```python
if name not in answers:        # answers is a DecisionResult
    ...
```

fails with `KeyError: 0` — an error that names neither the question, nor the key the caller used, nor the real problem.

## How it surfaced

Recipe 35's builder hit it while composing a six-feature `Noul` result and worked around it with `try`/`except`. The workaround is correct; the trap is that the natural spelling is wrong in a way the error message actively hides. A builder who has not seen it will spend real time on `KeyError(0)` before suspecting the container.

## Proposed fix

**Add `__contains__`**, so membership tests answer the question asked. Adding `__iter__` and a `keys()` alongside it would make the type behave like the mapping its `__getitem__` already implies, and would also stop the legacy-sequence fallback from ever being reached.

The alternative — removing `__getitem__` in favour of an explicit accessor — is more disruptive and loses a convenient spelling that works correctly today.

Either way the test is cheap and belongs with the fix: assert that `"some_name" in result` returns a bool for both a present and an absent name, and that it never raises `KeyError`.

## Why this is worth more than its size

It is the same shape as several other findings here: **a type that is half a mapping**, where the half that exists makes the missing half look present. The failure is not a crash at the boundary but a confusing error deep inside a caller's own code — and nothing in the repository would catch it, because no test exercises `in` against a `DecisionResult`.

Filed by the orchestrator from recipe 35's build report, with the attribute set measured directly rather than inferred.

title: Foundation: docs invite the [ml] extra for recipes that train a baseline, but the Tests jobs never install it and they import helpers.py
body:
`docs/notebook-ci.md` tells a recipe author to install the `[ml]` extra, and the notebook-execution workflow does install it — but **the two `Tests` jobs never do**, and they import every recipe's `helpers.py`. So a recipe that uses `[ml]` in `helpers.py` **passes notebook execution and fails both `Tests` legs**.

I verified each half directly:

- `.github/workflows/ci.yml:35` → `pip install -e ".[dev]"`, and `:77` → `pip install -e ".[dev,live]"` for the 3.14 leg. **Never `[ml]`.**
- `.github/workflows/notebooks.yml:119` → `pip install -e ".[ml]" -c .github/constraints-notebooks.txt`.
- `docs/notebook-ci.md:538` → tells a recipe author to run `pip install -e ".[ml]" -c .github/constraints-notebooks.txt`, and (per the builder that hit this) describes the extra as existing "for the recipes that train a baseline".
- `tests/test_helpers.py` in each recipe imports that recipe's `helpers.py`, and those tests run under the `Tests` jobs.

So the documentation points an author at an extra the test jobs do not have, for exactly the use case — training a baseline — that most invites putting the dependency in `helpers.py` where it can be tested.

## How it surfaced, and why it did not become a failure

Recipe 35 (#237) trains a classifier and compares it with a fixed baseline. Its builder was asked to settle the dependency question **before** writing the classifier, and found this boundary. It chose a plain-Python Bernoulli Naive Bayes over boolean vectors — `math.log`, no imports beyond the standard library — so nothing in `helpers.py` needs `[ml]`.

That was the right call and the recipe is fine. **The trap is still there for the next builder**, who will read `docs/notebook-ci.md`, see that `[ml]` exists for recipes that train a baseline, use scikit-learn in `helpers.py`, watch notebook execution pass, and then fail two required checks for a reason the documentation actively misled them about.

## What to decide

Three coherent resolutions, in rough order of cost:

1. **Document the boundary precisely.** `[ml]` may be imported **only inside notebook cells**, never in `helpers.py`, `build_fixtures.py` or any `tests/` module, because those are imported by jobs that do not install it. That is one paragraph in `docs/notebook-ci.md` next to the existing instruction, and it is worth doing whichever of the others is chosen.
2. **Install `[ml]` in the `Tests` jobs too**, so the extra is usable where it is natural. Costs CI time on every run for a dependency few recipes need, and widens what a test-time import can reach.
3. **Guard it**: a check that no `recipes/*/helpers.py`, `build_fixtures.py` or `tests/*.py` imports anything only available under `[ml]`. Decidable statically, and it would fail at the commit that introduces the problem rather than in CI — the pattern this repository has converged on for every other gap of this shape.

My own preference is 1 plus 3: say the rule where it is read, and enforce it where it is broken. Note that 1 alone leaves a documented rule with no mechanical check, which is the shape of five other open issues here.

## Worth noting about the current state

No published recipe is affected — nothing in any `recipes/*/helpers.py` needs `[ml]` today, which is why this has never fired. It is a latent trap created by documentation that is more inviting than the CI it describes, and recipe 35 is the first recipe that came close enough to find it.

Filed by the orchestrator from recipe 35's build report, with both workflow files and the docs line read directly.

title: Foundation: the validation-metric-line guard keys on formatting idioms, not the printed value (one false negative, two safe false positives)
body:
`tests/test_recipe_guard.py::test_validation_metric_lines_carry_selection_and_check` surprised one recipe's builder and reviewers **three separate times in a single pull request** (#226). Each surprise was caught, each by a human rather than by anything mechanical, and the next builder will not have two reviewers watching.

There is no issue for this guard today — #227 covers the reason-string guard and #211 the glossary rule — so the reviewer that found all three deliberately left the filing to a foundation call rather than scoping it itself.

## The three trigger quirks, with what each means

**1. Concatenated suffix → false positive. Acceptable; keep it.** A line that builds its `{selection}{check}` suffix by concatenation rather than literal placeholders **fails**, though the printed result is correct. That is the **safe** direction and it keeps one spelling across 31 recipes. Recorded explicitly so nobody "fixes" it into permissiveness.

**2. Hoisted format string → false negative. This is the real hole.** The check only inspects a `print(` whose call **contains a float format spec**. Move the formatting one line up and the line becomes invisible:

```python
val_wrong_text = f"{some_metric:.2f}"                    # formatting lives here
print(f"  wrongly selected anyway: {val_wrong_text}")    # no float spec inside the call
```

Measured on that recipe's cell: of three validation metric lines, **the middle one is not inspected**, and its labels are present only because the builder put them there. So a recipe that hoists its formatting can print an **unlabelled validation metric** straight past the one guard that exists for this — and a builder would do it not deliberately but because the line got long.

**3. A line containing the literal word "validation" → false positive.** A reworked print tripped the guard merely by containing that word, with no metric in it. Safe direction again, but it is the third distinct surprise in one guard, and it cost a round-trip.

## Why the three together are the point

Two false positives in the safe direction and one false negative that matters. The pattern is that the guard's **trigger** is a set of **formatting idioms** rather than the **property** — which is the same structure as four other findings this month: a citation check matching two literal spellings, a reason-string check matching a substring anywhere in a file, a plot/print check satisfied by the statement that destroys the figure, and this. Every one certifies the letter while the substance goes unenforced or over-enforced.

## Proposed fix

**Key the check on the printed value, not on the source idiom that produced it** — trace simple local bindings into the `print` call. The recipe guard **already does this for a sibling check**: its own check table describes a metric-line check as working "traced through simple bindings". So the machinery exists in the module and this trigger simply does not use it.

That single change fixes quirk 2 directly. Quirk 3 would also improve, since tracing a binding makes "does this line print a metric" answerable without keying on the word. Quirk 1 can stay as it is, deliberately.

## Audit before fixing, as usual here

Sweep the published set for validation metric lines that **hoist their formatting** and are therefore currently uninspected, and report the count before changing the check. Two issues this month were filed believing three recipes were affected; one audit found 25 of 27. The expectation here is a small number — the idiom only appears when a line gets long — but the expectation is not the measurement.

Filed by the orchestrator from #226's fifth and sixth review rounds, with all three quirks observed on committed code and the sibling check's "traced through simple bindings" wording confirmed in the guard module's own documentation.

title: Foundation: the template tells readers every number carries the run mode, which is false for demo answer and per-example lines (32 notebooks)
body:
`recipes/_template/notebook.ipynb`'s `setup-md` cell ends:

> The header states which mode ran, and **every number below carries that mode with it.**

That sentence is **false as written**, and it is in **32 notebooks** — all 31 published recipes plus the template. I verified the count directly (`git grep -l "carries that mode" origin/main -- 'recipes/*/notebook.ipynb'`).

## Why it is false

The `{check}`/`{selection}` suffixes that carry the mode are applied to **printed metric lines**. They are not applied to:

- the demo `show_answer(...)` blocks, which print an individual answer's choice, probabilities and confidence; or
- the per-example demo lines in the rule cells (`python-rule` and its equivalents), which print one example's decision.

Those are numbers below the header that do **not** carry the mode with them. So a reader who takes the sentence literally — which is how it is written, and the honesty rule in `CONTRIBUTING.md` section 2 is exactly about not writing more than is true — will find counterexamples within a few cells.

## Why this is template text rather than any recipe's defect

Found by #226's reviewer, which **checked before reporting it**: the sentence is identical in `recipes/_template` and in every published recipe it sampled. I confirmed the 32-notebook count. So no builder wrote it, no reviewer could reasonably have been expected to challenge boilerplate that predates the whole set, and fixing it in one recipe would make that recipe the odd one out.

It is also the cheapest possible fix: **one sentence in the template**, then the same sentence wherever it has already been copied. The honest version is barely longer — something to the effect that the header states which mode ran and **every reported metric** carries that mode with it, which is both true and still says the thing the sentence exists to say.

## One related question, which I checked and can close

The same reviewer noted that the phrase "true by construction" had travelled into recipe 28 from `17-passage-reranking`, and flagged that it had not verified whether recipe 17's own version holds. **I checked: it is a different claim and it is sound.** Recipe 17's `ranking-discuss` says a lexical-overlap gap "is true by construction, not a result", because every stored answer in its fixtures was written from its gold label. That is a statement about fixture authoring, and it is true. It is **not** the infeasible-threshold claim that is a must-change on #226. So there is no second instance to chase.

## Suggested handling

This is a one-line prose fix across 32 notebooks, and markdown-only — so it invalidates no committed output and needs no notebook re-execution, which puts it in the same cheap category as the wave close-out backlink sweep. Worth doing in the same pass rather than as its own round, and worth doing in the **template first** so the remaining 29 recipes are generated correctly.

Filed by the orchestrator from #226's review, with the count measured and the recipe-17 question resolved before filing.

title: Foundation: a committed figure can vanish with every check green, and print_what_you_plot encourages the edit that does it
body:
A committed figure can disappear from a notebook with **every check in the repository still green**, and the `print_what_you_plot` guard is what pushes a builder toward the edit that does it.

## The mechanism

`src/jev_cookbook/style.py` registers a PNG formatter for `Figure` on the running shell's **display formatter** (`_register_notebook_display`, `shell.display_formatter.formatters["image/png"].for_type(Figure, _figure_png)`). A display formatter renders the **cell result** — the value of the cell's last expression. So a cell ending in

```python
plot_risk_coverage(...)
```

commits a PNG, and a cell ending in

```python
plot_risk_coverage(...)
print(f"split overlap: {overlap:.4f}{check}")
```

commits **none**, because the Figure is no longer the cell result. No error, no warning.

Then the three checks that might notice all pass:

- **`print_what_you_plot` (G1(e))** requires "a `print` of the plotted object itself or of something a loop over it prints, **in the same code cell**". It is satisfied *by the very statement that removes the figure* — and, worse, it is the check that encourages adding prints to plotting cells in the first place.
- **Notebook freshness** compares committed outputs against a fresh execution. A fresh run emits no PNG either, so the notebook is perfectly fresh. This is the "a check can pass for two different reasons" shape again: identical outputs are equally the signature of nothing-changed and nothing-produced.
- **Hygiene, ruff, the validator and both suites** have no opinion about image outputs.

## Measured instance

Recipe 32's fix round (#230). I verified both heads myself:

| head | committed `image/png` outputs | total base64 bytes |
|---|---|---|
| `97427ab9` (before) | **2** | 78,944 |
| `c79a4c5a` (after) | **1** | 35,748 |

A 43,196-byte risk-coverage chart vanished because a `print` was appended after the `plot_risk_coverage(...)` call. Found by that pull request's reviewer; CI was green on the head that lost it.

## Audit of the published set: clean, which is the useful part

I measured every published recipe on `main` — for each code cell, the number of `plot_confusion_matrix`/`plot_threshold_sweep`/`plot_risk_coverage` calls against whether that cell has a committed `image/png` output:

**All 31 published recipes: zero plotting cells without a committed image.**

So there is **no backlog to clean up**, and that is why this is worth fixing now rather than later: the gap is latent, recipe 32 would have been the **first** recipe to ship a missing figure, and it was caught by a human-equivalent reading rather than by any check. The next one may not be.

## Proposed fix

Add a guard check: **every code cell containing a `plot_*` call must have at least one committed `image/png` output.** Decidable from the committed notebook with no execution, in the same family as the existing cell-level checks, and it would have failed on `c79a4c5a` immediately.

Two details worth getting right:

1. **Count per cell, not per notebook.** A notebook-level total would pass a cell that lost its figure while another cell gained one.
2. Consider pairing it with the inverse for `plot_answer_probabilities`, which also emits figures and is excluded from G1(e)'s list — the check should cover whatever actually produces an image rather than only the three evaluation helpers.

## Related, and worth a sentence in the style docs regardless of the guard

The underlying trap is that **a plotting helper's figure reaches the notebook only as the cell result**, so statement order inside a plotting cell is load-bearing. `docs/notebook-style.md`'s "Print what you plot" instruction asks for a print in the same cell without saying it must come **before** the plot call — which is the one thing a builder needs to know to avoid this. That sentence costs nothing and would have prevented the instance above.

Filed by the orchestrator from #230's review, with the mechanism read in `style.py`, the two-head figure counts measured directly, and the published-set audit run before filing rather than after.

title: Foundation: recall_at_budget credits ineligible candidates, so a gated rule's task-level recall can be a number the rule never produces
body:
`jev_cookbook.evaluation.recall_at_budget` has no concept of an **eligible** candidate. It fills its budget purely by score from the whole list it is given:

```python
return float(_tie_averaged(sc, rel)[: min(budget, len(rel))].sum() / total)
```

So any rule that **excludes** candidates before ranking — a confidence gate, a foreign-option check, a type or permission filter — cannot report its own recall through this helper without care, because the helper will happily credit a candidate the rule excluded.

## How it was found, and what it produced

Recipe 32 (#230, in review) selects a regression suite: one `Score` per candidate test, a confidence gate, then Python proposes a suite under a size budget. Its builder's first implementation passed a disclosed stand-in score for excluded candidates plus the raw `SUITE_BUDGET`.

On a patch with only **one** eligible candidate and a budget of 2, the helper silently credited the second slot to whichever excluded candidate tied for the next-highest stand-in score — **sometimes the exact candidate the confidence gate existed to exclude**. The reported recall was `0.6667` where the rule's own pick gives `0.5`.

That is the dangerous shape: not a crash, not a `NaN`, but **a plausible number that the recipe's own composition never produces**. Nothing in the repository would have flagged it.

## How the builder caught it, which is the part worth generalising

It wrote a test asserting that recall must equal `propose_suite`'s own pick **on every one of the 38 scored patches**, and ran it *before* trusting any task-level number. The test failed on the gate-type patches until it added an `effective_budget` helper capping the budget at the number of actually-eligible candidates for that specific patch.

**The invariant is the fix, not the helper**: a task-level metric must equal what the rule's own composition produces, checked on every committed example. That is the same move that closed several guard defects this month — compare against what the system actually does, not against a re-derivation that happens to look right.

## Why this belongs in the shared package

The builder solved it correctly inside its recipe and reported the gap rather than quietly working around it, which is the right behaviour. But `effective_budget`/`effective_scores` live in **one recipe's** `helpers.py`, and the shape — *a gate excludes a high-scoring candidate from a tight budget* — is not exotic. It is the natural structure of several remaining use cases (suite selection under budget, reviewer assignment under capacity, retrieval under a cost ceiling, paging under a context limit). The next builder to hit it will hit the identical trap, and the failure mode is a wrong number rather than an error, so the odds of catching it are whatever the odds are that someone writes that invariant test unprompted.

## Proposed fix

1. **Either** give `recall_at_budget` (and `mean_recall_at_budget`) an explicit `eligible` argument, so ineligible candidates can never occupy a budget slot — the honest signature for what callers actually need;
2. **or** document, loudly, in both docstrings that the caller must pass only eligible candidates **and** cap the budget at their count, with the recipe-32 failure as the worked example of what happens otherwise.

I prefer (1), because (2) is a rule that has to be remembered at exactly the moment a builder is thinking about something else, and the symptom is a number that looks fine. Note that the docstring is currently silent on the question rather than wrong — it says "A `budget` larger than the list is treated as the whole list", which is about the list it is given and reads as reassuring in precisely the case that bites.

3. **Audit** the published recipes that use either helper with a rule that excludes candidates, the way this repository has learned to: measure first, report the count, then fix. Recipe 17 (passage reranking) and any ranking recipe with a gate are the places to look.

## Related

The invariant the builder wrote — task-level metric equals the composition's own pick, on every committed example — is worth considering as a house standard for any recipe reporting a task-level metric, independently of this helper. It would have caught this, and it is cheap.

Filed by the orchestrator from recipe 32's build report, with the helper's source read and the absence of an eligibility concept confirmed directly.

title: Foundation: some recipes' test split is a near-duplicate of validation, so the held-out set is not held out
body:
Some recipes' `test` split is a near-duplicate of their `validation` split, so the held-out set is not meaningfully held out — and nothing in the repository measures or forbids it.

## The measurement

Found during recipe 28's review (#226), which fingerprinted stored answers across **all 30 published recipes** plus that one:

| recipe | share of `test` answers also in `validation` |
|---|---|
| **28-skill-selection** (in review) | **0.957** — 21 of 23 task profiles byte-identical |
| **17-passage-reranking** (published) | **0.900** |
| repository median | **≈ 0.16** |

Recipe 28's two splits consequently report the **identical** accuracy `0.9500` and risk `0.0500`. That is not a coincidence to be noted beside the number; it is close to arithmetic.

I am attributing rather than claiming this measurement: it is the reviewer's, with its method stated (per-task answer profiles compared byte-for-byte across splits). I have not independently reproduced the 0.957 and 0.900 figures, and the first thing to do with this issue is reproduce them.

## Why it matters more than a fixture-quality nit

The whole point of the validation/test discipline in this cookbook — `docs/evaluation.md`'s selective-prediction section, every recipe's "threshold frozen from validation, reported on test" structure — is that the reported numbers come from data the threshold did not see. `select_confidence_threshold` is documented as "Call this on validation data only, then report with `evaluate_selective` on test data using the returned value unchanged."

If the test split's answers are 96% the same as validation's, the threshold **has** effectively seen the test data, and the reported figure is close to a training-set number wearing a held-out label. Every recipe teaches a reader to do this properly. A recipe doing it improperly teaches the opposite while appearing to comply, and no check fires.

This also explains a pattern that has been read as reassuring: when a recipe's validation and test metrics land on identical values, that has generally been treated as the fixture set being balanced. On these two recipes it is instead a symptom.

## Why it was not blocked on #226, and why that was right

Recipe 28's reviewer declined to make it a must-change for a reason I agree with: **recipe 17 is that recipe's own named ancestor and the pattern it was told to reuse**, and recipe 17 is already published at 0.900. Blocking recipe 28 for inheriting a published recipe's pattern would hold one builder responsible for a set-wide decision nobody has written down. It flagged it for the orchestrator instead, which is how a set-wide finding should surface.

It also named the consequence of ruling the other way, plainly: **if held-out independence becomes a contract requirement, recipe 28 fails it and so does recipe 17** — a published recipe. That is the real decision in this issue, and it is the owner's.

## What to decide, and then what to check

1. **Is a meaningfully distinct `test` split a contract requirement?** My view: yes in substance, because without it the central discipline the cookbook teaches is not being practised in the recipes that teach it. But it is a contract change affecting a published recipe, so it is not mine to make.
2. **If yes, set a threshold and justify it.** A share-of-identical-answers ceiling is the obvious form. The repository median near 0.16 suggests most recipes are comfortably clear, so a ceiling well above the median — but far below 0.9 — would catch the outliers without churning the set.
3. **Then audit, the way this repository has learned to**: measure across all published recipes, report the count, and only then fix. Two issues this month were filed believing three recipes were affected; one audit found 25 of 27. Here the reviewer's sweep suggests exactly two outliers, which would be a pleasantly small result — treat a larger one as the interesting outcome.
4. **A guard is decidable.** The comparison is over committed fixtures with no execution needed, which puts it in the same cheap category as the backlink audit and makes it a candidate for the `catalog_audit` close-out marker rather than a per-pull-request check.

## Related

The same review established that recipe 28's identical cross-split figures are **not** explained by the mirroring alone, so this is additional to, not a substitute for, the unfalsifiable-metric rule that `CONTRIBUTING.md` section 2 and the house standard already require. A recipe could have well-separated splits and still report a construction-perfect number, and vice versa.

Filed by the orchestrator from #226's review. The recipe under review is not being asked to fix it.

title: Foundation: the confidence-gate reason-string guard proves a string is present, not that a live review branch produces it
body:
`tests/test_recipe_guard.py::test_the_confidence_gate_reason_string_is_exact` is two lines:

```python
text = (recipe_dir(recipe) / "helpers.py").read_text("utf-8")
assert REASON_STRING in text
```

applied via `guarded_with_template("review_reason_string")()` to **every** recipe and the template, with no exemption mechanism. `REASON_STRING` is `"confidence below the threshold"`.

The rule it enforces is a wording rule, and a good one — `docs/glossary.md#review`: *"the reason string for a confidence-gated review is exactly 'confidence below the threshold', so two recipes' readers see the same words for the same cause."* That is a rule about **how a confidence-gated review is worded**. The check is an unconditional substring search, so in practice it enforces something quite different and much stronger: **every recipe must have a confidence-gated review at all.**

## How it surfaced

Recipe 28 (#28, PR #226) is a `Score` recipe whose rule, as its issue specifies it, is *"Python selects the top skill when the score and the margin are sufficient, and otherwise requests clarification."* Score and margin. No per-answer confidence check anywhere in the decision rule the issue describes.

Its builder could not pass the guard. The two ways out:

1. Add the literal string as dead text — a comment, or an unused constant. **This passes**, because the check is a plain substring search over the file's full text, deliberately not restricted to code (the docstring explains that choice, reasonably, since the string is a literal argument in the rule's own code rather than prose).
2. Add a real confidence gate the use case did not ask for.

The builder chose (2) and did it properly — its own pool, its own selector, its own mutation-proof test, and a fixture case it actually catches on `validation` — then reported the cascade honestly: the margin pool had to stay filtered by cutoff only, **not** by confidence, or it would have lost its one wrong example and become vacuous. That is a good outcome for recipe 28 and the right call by that builder. It is not a good outcome for the guard, because the recipe's decision rule now contains a third stage that exists because a check demanded it.

## Why this is worth fixing before the remaining 32 recipes

This guard **shapes content rather than checking it**, and it will keep doing so. Plenty of the remaining use cases are ranking, scoring, or selection rules where a confidence gate is not the natural review branch — the issues describe margins, budgets, top-k cutoffs, interlocks, retry limits. Each of those builders faces the same two options, and option (1) is cheaper. A dead string in a comment satisfying a guard about the *wording of a real mechanism* is the worst version of this: the check stays green while meaning nothing, which is the #215 pattern.

So the defect runs both ways:

- **Over-mandates:** a recipe with no confidence-gated review cannot pass without inventing one.
- **Under-verifies:** a recipe *with* one can pass by having the words anywhere in the file, including in a comment, with no binding to the rule's own review branch.

`CONTRIBUTING.md` section 4's exemption machinery and the glossary's own "a recipe may still name its own domain-specific sub-reasons" show the contract already contemplates rules whose review branch is not a confidence gate. The guard does not.

There is precedent for the fix shape in this same module: `test_review_outcome_value_is_review_where_it_exists` is conditional — *"checked directly where `helpers.py` defines a module-level `REVIEW` constant; traced where it…"* — and carries a named, justified exemption (`16-discord-moderation-triage`, `ESCALATE` as a genuine domain outcome rather than `REVIEW` renamed). The reason-string check should be conditional in the same way.

## Proposed fix

1. **Make it conditional on the recipe having a confidence gate**: if the rule has no per-answer confidence comparison, the check does not apply — and should say so rather than skip silently, the way the module's other conditional checks do.
2. **Bind it to the gate when there is one**, instead of searching the whole file: the string must be the reason on the branch the confidence comparison controls. `CONFIDENCE_REASON_PREFIX` already exists in this module for exactly this tracing (`(\w+)\s*,\s*"confidence below`), so most of the machinery is present.
