3. **Audit the published set** for recipes that satisfy this check with a string not bound to a confidence branch — the #215 discipline: measure first, report the count, then fix. The two directions above make that a cheap query once (2) exists.

## Also worth deciding

Recipe 28's added gate should probably stay regardless — it is genuine, consequential and tested. But that is a judgement for its reviewer, not a consequence of this issue. Flagging it so nobody later reads the gate as padding and removes it without understanding why it is there; and conversely, so its review examines whether it earns its place on the merits rather than because a guard required it.

Filed by the orchestrator from recipe 28's build report, with the guard source read and the claim confirmed directly.

title: Foundation: the no_issue_citations guard is narrower than CONTRIBUTING section 6 (PR-description and house-rule citations pass)
body:
`CONTRIBUTING.md` section 6 says: *"A recipe file never cites a private issue number or 'the issue' — a reader cannot see either."* The stated reason is **what the reader can see**. The guard that enforces it, `no_issue_citations` (`tests/test_recipe_guard.py`, `test_no_issue_numbers_or_the_issue_in_recipe_files`), detects only `#NNN` and the literal phrase "the issue".

So every other way of citing something a reader cannot see passes.

## Found in review, not by the guard

PR #223 (recipe 30) added four comment lines in `recipes/30-citation-verification/tests/test_helpers.py` that cite documents outside the repository, and CI stayed green on all 10 checks:

| line | citation | what a reader can see |
|---|---|---|
| 51 | "…the **PR description** proves against…" | nothing — and the pointer dangles the moment the pull request merges |
| 278 | "Fixture-generation consistency (**Wave 3 batch 1 rule 11**)" | nothing — this numbering exists in no file in the repository |
| 320 | "proved in the **PR description** by the corresponding mutation" | nothing |
| 471 | "**Rule 12**: nothing in this file pins…" | nothing |

`Wave 3` appears nowhere in the tree except `orchestration/PROMPT.md`. "Batch 1 rule 11" and "Rule 12" are house review-brief numbering that exists only in an orchestration working file. A reader who clones this repository and opens that test file is told the proof lives somewhere they cannot reach.

By contrast, `strong-form guard (G1(c))` in the same file is **fine** and should not be caught: `G1(c)` is defined in `tests/test_recipe_guard.py` and `docs/notebook-ci.md`, both in the tree.

## Why this is the same shape as #215

The rule was never wrong and the guard was never missing — the **detection was narrower than the rule it names**, so the property went unenforced in every form but the two spelled out. #215 was exactly this: a documented contract requirement whose only test could not fail for the thing it named, and the audit then found 25 of 27 recipes in breach. That is the reason to widen this one before the remaining 32 recipes are written rather than after.

A pull-request description is the worst case of the class, because it is the one citation target that is **guaranteed** to become unreachable: squash-merge discards the branch, and the body survives only as a commit message nobody reading a test file will find.

## Proposed detection

Add to the same guard, over the same prose scope it already walks (`helpers.py`, `build_fixtures.py`, every `tests/*.py`, `README.md`, notebook markdown and code-cell comments/docstrings, quoted fixture text stripped as now):

- `PR description`, `pull request description`, `pull request body`, `the PR`, `this PR`, `PR #`
- `Wave <n>`, `batch <n>`, `round <letter-or-number>` used as a process reference
- `rule <n>` / `Rule <n>` — house brief numbering, which exists in no committed file
- `the orchestrator`, `the brief`, `the reviewer` where used as the authority for a claim

With one deliberate carve-out, which is the whole trick to getting this right: a citation **is** allowed when its target is a committed file — `G1(c)`, `CONTRIBUTING.md section 6`, `docs/evaluation.md`, `R21`. The cheap, non-clever form is a reference-anchor allowlist of the identifiers the repository actually defines, and anything else that looks like a cross-reference is a hit.

## Audit before landing, and please do it the #215 way

Do not fix the four lines in #223 and close this. Run the widened detection across **all** published recipes first and report the count. #215 was filed believing three recipes were affected; the audit found **25 of 27**. The same could be true here — these briefs have been handing builders rule numbers all night, and a builder citing the number it was briefed with is the predictable outcome rather than a surprise.

Note also that the orchestration briefs are the upstream cause: they number house rules, so a conscientious builder cites that numbering in a comment explaining *why* a test exists. The brief has been corrected to say "state the property, never the rule number" — but a guard is what makes it stick, which is the whole argument of #218.

Filed by the orchestrator from the #223 re-review. The four lines in #223 are being fixed in that pull request as a must-change; this issue is for the detection gap, which outlives them.

title: Foundation: four set-wide gaps from the recipe 25 review (queue attribution, threshold binding, forced-metric disclosure, baseline template line)
body:
Four set-wide gaps the Opus review of PR #221 (recipe 25) found while reviewing a single recipe. Each affects **every published recipe** or **every remaining builder**, so each wants one decision applied everywhere rather than a per-recipe fix. Grouped because they share that shape; they are otherwise independent and can be taken separately.

## 1. A published recipe records a misleading answer in its review queue

Recipe 25's `queue-build` recorded `answer=decide(example)["implementation_evidence"]` as "the typed answer that sent the item to review" — but on **8 of its 12** queued records the gate was tripped by a *different* proposition, so the recorded answer sat at confidence 0.92–0.94 and had nothing to do with why the item was queued. That is being fixed in #221.

**The same defect is already published in recipe 26**: `queue.submit(item, result.reason, answer=decide(example)["redirect"])` always records the `redirect` answer regardless of which label tripped the gate. Nobody has checked the other multi-label recipes.

What to do: audit every published recipe that queues a multi-label decision, and either record the answer that actually caused the gating or stop labelling it as the cause. A reader is being told *this answer is why this item needs review*, and on most of those rows it is not true.

## 2. Threshold selection is duplicated between every notebook and its tests

Every published recipe re-derives its thresholds inside its own tests rather than binding them to what the notebook computes. The consequence the reviewer drew out: **no test can fail if a notebook changes its `objective` or `target_accuracy`.** The consequentiality proofs — the tests that show a proposition genuinely matters — are therefore proving something about a procedure the notebook may no longer run.

Recipe 25 factors this better than the four recipes before it, which is why it was visible. Options the reviewer named: a `helpers.freeze_thresholds(...)` convention, or a shared helper in `jev_cookbook`. Decide once; 34 recipes remain.

## 3. Wave rule 3 — "a metric that cannot come out otherwise is reported as such" — is unimplemented set-wide

Validation accuracy `1.0000` and risk `0.0000` under `target_accuracy=1.0` are **forced by construction** in recipes 24, 25, 26, 27 and 29 alike. All five label them only "(a selection step, not a reported result)", which says where the number came from but not that it could not have come out otherwise.

This is the rule #208 carries as contract text. A single template sentence would close it in every recipe at once, and would stop each reviewer having to rediscover it per recipe — which is what has happened five times now.

## 4. The pull-request template forces a vacuous tick on baseline-free recipes

`CONTRIBUTING.md` section 6 already makes the baseline conditional: "compare with the baseline the issue names **when there is one**." But the pull-request template's line reads as an unconditional assertion — "Evaluation against gold labels, with the baseline the issue names" — so a builder of a recipe whose issue names no baseline must either tick something inapplicable or hand-annotate it.

Recipe 25's builder annotated it, which was right, and its reviewer ruled that the contract resolves the question and **issue #25 should not be amended** — the defect is in the template. Rephrasing the line to "…and with the baseline the issue names, **if any**" is a one-line change that removes the problem for all 34 remaining recipes.

A separate question, worth deciding deliberately rather than by omission: **should Level 3 recipes name a baseline at all?** A reader currently cannot tell whether recipe 25's gap-list exact match of 0.9231 is good. That is a contract and template decision, not a per-issue amendment.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Every published multi-label recipe's queue records the answer that actually caused the gating, or stops calling it the cause; recipe 26 specifically is fixed.
- [ ] Threshold selection is bound between notebook and tests by one decided mechanism, so changing a notebook's `objective` or `target_accuracy` fails a test.
- [ ] The forced-metric disclosure of wave rule 3 is in the template and applied to the five recipes that currently carry an undisclosed forced metric.
- [ ] The pull-request template's baseline line is conditional, matching `CONTRIBUTING.md` section 6.
- [ ] A recorded decision on whether Level 3 recipes should name a baseline, either way.

title: Foundation: CONTRIBUTING section 2, the honesty rule, has no mechanical check at all
body:
`CONTRIBUTING.md` section 2 — no notebook, README or pull request may state or imply anything about Jev's real quality, latency or cost except as measured on N examples with the returned model version and capture date — is **the one central rule in this repository with no mechanical check at all**. Found and demonstrated by the Opus review of PR #206, comment 6105573346.

## The demonstration

The reviewer inserted a fabricated claim about Jev's quality into recipe 26's `measured-md` cell and ran the checks. **All thirteen of recipe 26's guards passed.** Lint, format, hygiene, the fixture validator, the catalog check, the notebook freshness check, the per-recipe guard family — none of them looks at whether the prose makes a claim the evidence cannot support.

So the rule that exists to stop this cookbook making false public statements about a real commercial product is enforced by exactly one thing: a reviewer reading carefully and knowing to look.

## Why this is the most consequential unguarded rule, not just another one

Tonight's reviews found several unguarded conventions — glossary links (#211), documentation facts (#216), matrix alignment (#217), the scaffolder's offline `N` (#215), notebook side effects (#212). Every one of those, if it slips, produces a worse cookbook. **This one, if it slips, produces a false claim about a vendor's product in published material.** The failure mode is categorically different, and the cost of a miss does not fall on us.

Three things make the risk concrete rather than theoretical:

- **Thirty-five recipes remain.** Every one will be built by a worker that has never read the others, and checked by a reviewer that must notice an overclaim among a few thousand words of prose.
- **The reviews have already caught real instances**, which is evidence the hazard is live, not hypothetical: #204's recipe README asserted that Jev "judg[es] from the evidence as a whole rather than trusting the tool's own reported status" — contradicted by the recipe's own fixture; #204 also presented a first-listed-option share as a check for model position bias, which offline measures only the fixture author (now #208); #206 reported a per-label F1 of 1.0000 that was perfect by construction. Each needed a reviewer to catch it, and each did — but a rule whose enforcement rate depends on reviewer attention has an unknown miss rate, and we have no way to measure it.
- **Every fixture in the repository is `synthetic`.** Authentic accepted live-recording coverage is **0 of 60**. So *every* number in *every* published recipe today is a pipeline check, and the only thing distinguishing an honest notebook from a dishonest one is prose that nothing verifies.

## What a check can and cannot do

It cannot judge meaning, and this issue should not pretend otherwise. But several mechanical approximations would each have caught real instances:

1. **Provenance-conditioned claim vocabulary.** Where a recipe's stored responses are all `model: "synthetic"`, flag prose in that recipe that uses the vocabulary of measured performance — accuracy or quality *of Jev* rather than of the pipeline, latency, cost, speed, "performs", "is good at", "reliably", "better than" — unless the sentence also carries the pipeline-check labelling the contract requires. Noisy, so make it a warning the author must answer in the pull request rather than a hard failure, or maintain an explicit allowlist of reviewed sentences.
2. **Require the labelling, which is the positive form and far more checkable.** Section 2 already says a synthetic number must be labelled a pipeline check beside it. That is close to mechanical: find the printed metrics in a notebook's committed outputs, and require the accompanying prose to carry the label. Absence of a label is detectable even when presence of a claim is not.
3. **Pin provenance against vocabulary.** A notebook that says `recorded` anywhere must have at least one stored response whose `model` is not `synthetic`; one whose responses are all synthetic must not use the recorded vocabulary at all. That is exactly checkable and closes the worst case — a recipe claiming measured results it never measured.
4. **A reviewer prompt in `REVIEWER_RULES.md`, kept whatever the guard does.** The guard will not judge meaning, so the manual check must stay, and it should say plainly that it is the **only** enforcement for the parts a check cannot reach.

## What to decide, and record

- Which approximations are worth their false-positive rate, and which are rejected and why. A rejected idea recorded is worth more than a silent omission.
- Whether a warning-with-answer is acceptable for a rule this important, or whether only a hard failure will do.
- What the guard explicitly does **not** cover, written where reviewers read it, so nobody mistakes a green check for an honesty guarantee.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The provenance-versus-vocabulary check (item 3) exists and fails closed; proved by mutation — add `recorded` vocabulary to an all-synthetic recipe and watch it fail.
- [ ] The labelling requirement (item 2) is enforced as far as it mechanically can be, with its limits written down.
- [ ] A decision is recorded on item 1, implemented or rejected with a reason.
- [ ] `REVIEWER_RULES.md` states which parts of section 2 have no mechanical check and remain the reviewer's sole responsibility.
- [ ] The guard is proved against the three real instances above, reconstructed as test cases: a README asserting Jev judges correctly, a fixture-derived statistic presented as evidence about the model, and a construction-perfect metric reported without caveat.
- [ ] The published set is swept once under whatever lands, and the result recorded here.
- [ ] Nothing in this work weakens or narrows section 2 itself; the contract is the standard and the check is the floor.

title: Foundation: the template's confusion-matrix print block misaligns when a count is wider than the widest label
body:
The confusion-matrix print block in `recipes/_template/notebook.ipynb` misaligns when a count has more digits than the widest class label. Latent today, but the template is copied by the **thirty-seven recipes that are not yet built**, so it is cheaper to fix in the template than in thirty-seven copies.

## The defect

The block sizes its columns from the widest label and formats counts with `f"{count:{width}d}"`. When a count's digit length exceeds `width`, Python's format spec does not truncate — the field simply grows — so that row's columns shift right and the matrix stops lining up under its header.

It is not reachable in the published set today: across all committed matrices the counts are single-digit while labels run 8 to 19 characters. It becomes reachable as soon as a recipe has a class with a hundred or more examples in one cell, or short labels — neither of which is exotic. Found by the Opus review of PR #199 (comment 6103947412), which demonstrated the misalignment, and confirmed by the #201 integration worker, which deliberately did **not** fix it because `recipes/_template/` was outside its allowed paths. That was the right call and is why this issue exists.

## History worth knowing, so this is fixed once

This formula has already been changed twice and the published set has carried three different forms:

- The original form misaligned for any label width other than 7.
- The template's current `max(...)` / `leader_width` form fixed that and is what recipes 01, 04, 05, 08, 09 and — as of #201 — 20 use. It still has the digit-width case above.
- Recipes 20 and 23 had reached alignment through a **second** formulation, `header_prefix = "  predicted ->".ljust(len("  gold ") + width + 2)`, correct in only one direction. #201 converged recipe 20 onto the template's form; **recipe 23 has not been converged** and should be checked here.

So the published set is nearly but not entirely on one formula, and the one it is converging on has a known hole. Fix the hole and finish the convergence together, rather than leaving a third round of this.

## What to do

1. Fix the template's block so column width is the maximum of the label width and the widest rendered count, and prove it with a case where a count is wider than every label.
2. Check `recipes/23-pairwise-answer-evaluation` and converge it onto the same form if it still carries the `ljust` formulation.
3. Propagate the corrected form to every published recipe that prints a matrix, so one formula is in use everywhere.
4. Guard it. There is currently **no recipe-level check for matrix alignment** — this is the `#165` gap a reviewer noted — so the obvious shape is a per-recipe test in the `tests/test_recipe_guard.py` family asserting that every printed matrix row aligns under its header, parametrised over published recipes. Prove it by mutation: widen one count past the label width and confirm it fails.
5. Note for whoever takes this: `tools/new_recipe.py` and the template must agree afterwards. Issue **#215** covers making template and scaffolder provably agree, and if that lands first this fix should ride on its mechanism rather than reintroducing two sources.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The template's matrix block aligns when a count is wider than the widest label, proved by a concrete case.
- [ ] Recipe 23 is checked and converged if needed; one formula is in use across every published recipe that prints a matrix.
- [ ] A per-recipe guard asserts matrix rows align under their header, proved by mutation.
- [ ] `tools/new_recipe.py` and the template agree on the corrected form.
- [ ] Preferably done before the Wave 3 batch 2 briefs, so new recipes copy the corrected form rather than needing a fourth sweep.

title: Foundation: documentation facts and the dash convention have no enforcement, so docs go stale silently
body:
**Two independent Opus reviewers converged on this without seeing each other's findings**, which is why it is worth doing rather than noting. From the two reviews of PR #199, comments 6104132790 and 6104183532.

## The problem, demonstrated rather than hypothesised

`docs/fixtures.md` said recipe 12's `shuffled_candidates` and recipe 23's `assign_first_shown` "predate this helper and migrate onto it separately (issue #163)". That was true when written. Then #196 and #192 merged, both recipes migrated onto the helper, and the sentence became **false** — in a contract document, contradicting a sentence three paragraphs above it in the same section, aimed at the thirty-seven builders who read that section to learn the convention.

Nothing caught it. Not CI, not the executable-docs-examples test (which reads one file, `docs/evaluation.md`), not `tests/test_style_docs.py` (which pins only `notebook-style.md`'s fenced blocks). It took two Opus reviewers, one grading it must-change and one a suggestion, plus an orchestrator adjudication, to fix one clause. One reviewer verified the gap empirically: it reverted both sentences and then replaced them with garbage strings, and the full suite returned byte-identical counts each time — 2898 passed / 2 skipped / 23 deselected. The documentation is simply not observed by any test.

That is an expensive mechanism for catching one stale clause, and it only worked because this pull request happened to carry two reviewers.

## Part 1 — pin the facts, not the prose

Both reviewers independently proposed the same remedy and both noted explicitly that pinning the **prose** is the wrong answer: wording should stay free to improve. What is checkable is the **claim**.

The corrected sentence now asserts two mechanically verifiable things: that `shuffled_candidates` and `assign_first_shown` are the two recipe-side shapes this convention takes, and which shared helper each uses. So:

- Assert that every recipe importing `stable_shuffle` or `stable_permutation` is named in that section, and that none is described as predating the helper. One reviewer noted this check **would have failed at the moment #196 merged** — the defect would have surfaced as a red test in #196's own pull request rather than three merges later.
- Assert each named function exists and uses the helper the document attributes to it.
- `tests/test_permutation.py` already cites this section by name and is the natural home; one reviewer put the cost at about three lines.

Then look for the same shape elsewhere. A documentation statement that names specific recipes, functions, or counts is a factual claim with a shelf life, and this repository's documents are full of them. Worth a survey rather than fixing only the one instance that happened to be caught.

## Part 2 — the dash convention has no enforcement at all

#164 established that prose uses an em dash rather than ` -- `. Nothing checks it, and the consequence is visible: **three** instances survived in `docs/fixtures.md` alone — the fix round found two and a reviewer found the third, at end of line, which a space-delimited grep had missed — and two remain in `docs/simulation.md:165` and `docs/backends.md:276` as sweep items.

A short test rejecting ` -- ` in markdown prose, outside fenced blocks and code spans, would close the class and make that sweep item self-closing. It has to respect the real exceptions, which already exist: `docs/development.md` has seven inside fenced shell blocks, `docs/notebook-style.md:25` is the convention quoting itself, `docs/fixtures.md:212` carries the `<!-- accepted-fake-credential -->` marker that `tests/test_fixtures.py:1340` keys off, and the repository's Python docstrings legitimately use ` -- `.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A test pins the factual claims of `docs/fixtures.md`'s "Per-item option order" section: every recipe using either helper is named, none is described as predating it, and each named function uses the attributed helper.
- [ ] That test is proved by mutation — reintroduce the stale "predates this helper" wording, or add a third recipe using a helper without naming it, and watch it fail.
- [ ] Other documentation statements naming specific recipes, functions or counts are surveyed, and the ones worth pinning are pinned or the decision not to is recorded.
- [ ] A test rejects ` -- ` in markdown prose outside fenced blocks and code spans, with the existing legitimate exceptions passing.
- [ ] `docs/simulation.md:165` and `docs/backends.md:276` are fixed under it, closing the #163 sweep item.
- [ ] Prose wording itself is **not** pinned; only checkable facts and the typographic convention.

title: Foundation: the scaffolder omits the offline N that the template and CONTRIBUTING require, and nothing makes the two agree
body:
Found by the Opus review of PR #199, comment 6103919778, and routed here rather than into that pull request. Filed with some urgency: of everything the reviews have surfaced, this is the largest remaining way a template-level defect propagates across the thirty-seven recipes that are not yet built, and it should be fixed **before the Wave 3 briefs go out**.

## The defect

`tools/new_recipe.py`'s generated `measured` cell **prints no `N` in the offline branch**, while `recipes/_template/notebook.ipynb` does and `CONTRIBUTING.md` section 2 requires it — no notebook may state or imply anything about Jev's quality, latency, or cost "except as measured on N examples". So every recipe produced by the scaffolder starts life missing a thing the contract requires, and the only test covering this reads `recipes/_template` alone, so no recipe-level guard catches it.

It is not hypothetical. Measured on current `main`: **recipes 21, 22 and 23 print no offline `N`.**

The cause is a half-landed fix. Issue #164's comment [6077629404](https://github.com/Jev-Engineering/cookbook/issues/164#issuecomment-6077629404) routed exactly this, and the **template** half landed; the **scaffolder** half never did. The template and the scaffolder are supposed to generate the same thing, and nothing checks that they agree.

## Why it compounds

Thirty-seven recipes remain. Each is scaffolded from `tools/new_recipe.py`, so each will start without the offline `N` and depend on its builder noticing and its reviewer catching it. Tonight's reviews show that is not a reliable mechanism: the same missing-glossary-link class was caught by eye on three separate recipes in one night, and the reason a guard was opened for it (#211) is precisely that eyes do not scale to sixty.

## What to do

1. Make the scaffolder's generated `measured` cell print `N` in the offline branch, matching the template.
2. **Make the template and the scaffolder provably agree**, which is the structural fix and the reason this is a foundation issue rather than a one-line patch. Today they are two sources that happen to say similar things, so a fix can land in one and not the other — exactly what happened here. Either generate from a single source or add a test asserting the generated skeleton matches the template on the properties that matter.
3. Add a recipe-level guard, in the family of `tests/test_recipe_guard.py`'s per-recipe checks, requiring every published recipe's `measured` cell to print `N` in its offline branch. The existing test reads only `recipes/_template`, which is why three published recipes drifted undetected.
4. Fix recipes 21, 22 and 23 through the normal reviewed pipeline, and re-measure the whole published set rather than trusting that list — it was found by one reviewer's spot measurement, not by an exhaustive audit.
5. Check whether anything else #164's comment 6077629404 routed landed in the template but not the scaffolder. One half-landed fix suggests the pairing was not systematic.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The scaffolder's generated `measured` cell prints `N` in the offline branch.
- [ ] Template and scaffolder agreement is enforced mechanically, not by convention; a test proves it fails when they diverge.
- [ ] A per-recipe guard requires the offline `N` for every published recipe, and fails when it is removed from one.
- [ ] Recipes 21, 22 and 23 are fixed, and the full published set is audited with the result recorded here.
- [ ] Any other half-landed item from #164 comment 6077629404 is identified and closed out.
- [ ] Done before the Wave 3 batch 2 briefs are issued, or the briefs explicitly carry the workaround.

title: Foundation: the wave close-out audit has no procedure that runs it
body:
PR #207 (merged as `3c25a2a98d276fb9f55d2143b45686f5851b4f72`) converted `next_steps_inbound_links` into a `catalog_audit`-marked **wave close-out audit**, deselected from per-pull-request runs and meant to be run deliberately at a wave's close. The check is correct and provably non-vacuous — two independent reviewers broke an inbound link and watched it go red while the default invocation stayed green. But its approving review (comment 6103261721, suggestion S2) found that **nothing in the repository ever runs it**, and that is worth fixing before it is forgotten.

## The gap

`close-out` appears only in the three lines #207 added. There is no workflow, no schedule, no issue template, and no wave close-out checklist anywhere that invokes the audit. `grep -rn -i wave docs/ CONTRIBUTING.md .github/` turns up only billing and parallelism prose plus one `merge-readiness.md` mention of Wave 0. So the audit runs if and only if a person remembers to type the command — which, for a check whose entire purpose is to catch a cross-recipe defect that no single pull request can see, means it will eventually not run at all.

`orchestration/PROMPT.md` does describe an "After each recipe wave" procedure (catalog audit, consistency review, close the level's tracking issue, progress comment on #80), but that file is the orchestration prompt rather than a repository procedure the audit can be attached to, and it does not name this command.

## What to do

1. Decide where a wave close-out procedure lives as a repository document, and write it. The natural content is what `orchestration/PROMPT.md` already describes — the catalog audit, the cross-recipe consistency review, the tracking-issue closure, and now this audit — stated as steps someone can follow.
2. Put the actual command in it, copy-pasteable, and say what a failure means and who fixes it.
3. Decide whether it should also run unattended. A scheduled run (the `Notebooks` workflow already has a weekly cron for a related reason) would catch the drift without depending on memory; if that is rejected, record why, so the decision is deliberate rather than an omission.
4. Consider making the audit's absence visible: if a wave's tracking issue (#75–#79) cannot be closed without the audit's output pasted into it, the procedure enforces itself.
5. Add the half-sentence from suggestion S3 while in `docs/development.md`: a node id alone does not re-select a deselected test, so `pytest tests/test_recipe_guard.py::test_...` reports `no tests ran (23 deselected)` rather than running it. That gotcha will cost someone an afternoon otherwise.

## A contract sentence that now needs a clause

`CONTRIBUTING.md` section 7 still says "Nothing is skipped, disabled, or loosened to get there." A reader can now hold that against a check that is deliberately deselected from every pull-request run. #203 authorised the change and both `docs/development.md` and `docs/notebook-ci.md` explain it honestly, so this is wording rather than substance — but the contract is the document reviewers are pointed at, and it should distinguish a check that was weakened from one that was deliberately moved to a different cadence. Fix it here or in whichever pull request next touches that section.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A wave close-out procedure exists as a repository document, naming the audit command and what to do when it fails.
- [ ] The decision on whether to run the audit unattended is recorded, either implemented or explicitly declined with a reason.
- [ ] `CONTRIBUTING.md` section 7 distinguishes a weakened check from one deliberately run at a different cadence.
- [ ] `docs/development.md` notes that a node id alone does not re-select a deselected test.
- [ ] Waves 1 and 2 are already closed; the audit is run once against current `main` and its output recorded here, so the procedure starts from a known state rather than an assumed one.

title: Foundation: no check that a recipe's live request count matches its README, or that no example is decided twice
body:
Nothing checks that a recipe's live request count matches what its README promises, or that a notebook does not decide the same example twice. Found by the Opus review of PR #205 (recipe 27), comment 6092760430, as must-change finding 1 — but the class of defect is repository-wide and this issue is for the guard, not that recipe's fix.

## Why this one is not cosmetic

It spends the owner's money and then fails. In recipe 27 the notebook decides `demo-02` in both the `answer` cell and the `python-rule` cell, so a live run makes **41** requests. Its README states "exactly 40 … each decided once" and instructs the reader to set `JEV_COOKBOOK_LIVE_MAX_REQUESTS=40`. Follow that instruction and the budget guard raises `BudgetExceeded` on the final `test` request — **after** forty requests have already been paid for. The reviewer verified it by instrumenting `ReplayBackend.decide`: 41 calls, 40 distinct keys, `demo-02` twice. `LiveBackend.decide` has no cache, so replay hides what live would charge for.

This lands directly on the $25 cumulative recording grant ([#80 comment 6025510672](https://github.com/Jev-Engineering/cookbook/issues/80#issuecomment-6025510672)). A recipe whose stated request count understates its real one makes the whole budget arithmetic wrong, and the error is invisible offline, which is precisely where every recipe is built and reviewed. With sixty recipes to record, a per-recipe undercount is a systematic overspend, not a rounding error.

The discipline currently exists only as prose: the template tells authors "the first answer is the one shown above, so it is not requested a second time". Recipe 27's builder read that and still shipped the duplicate, which is what prose rather than a check gets you.

## What to do

1. Add a check that counts the decisions a notebook actually makes per recipe — instrumenting the backend during the offline execution CI already performs is the cheap route, since replay and live take the same path through `decide` — and compares it against a single declared number for that recipe.
2. Decide where the declared number lives so it is one value, not prose repeated in the README and the notebook that can drift apart. Whatever is chosen, the README's stated count and its suggested `JEV_COOKBOOK_LIVE_MAX_REQUESTS` must be derived from it rather than written by hand.
3. Fail on a duplicate decision of the same example as its own condition, with the offending key named, since that is the specific mistake here and it is cheaper to detect than a count mismatch.
4. Confirm the arithmetic the guard protects: that `JEV_COOKBOOK_LIVE_MAX_REQUESTS` as documented is an inclusive cap the stated count does not exceed, so following the README cannot abort a run mid-way.
5. Audit every published recipe for both conditions and record the counts here. Any recipe whose README overstates or understates its real request count is a live-budget correction, so this audit should finish before any further live recording is authorized.
6. Fix the drift found through the normal reviewed pipeline, not inside recipe pull requests open for other purposes.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A per-recipe check counts actual decisions during offline notebook execution and fails on a mismatch with the declared number.
- [ ] A duplicate decision of the same example fails the check on its own, naming the key.
- [ ] The declared count has exactly one source, and the README's count and budget instruction are derived from it.
- [ ] Following a recipe README's documented budget cannot abort that recipe's own run.
- [ ] Every published recipe is audited for both conditions, with the counts recorded here.
- [ ] Any correction needed to the $25 budget arithmetic is stated on #80 before further live recording.

title: Foundation: no check verifies a recipe's notebook actually invokes its simulated side effect
body:
Nothing in the repository verifies that a recipe's notebook actually **invokes** its simulated side effect. Found and demonstrated by the Opus re-review of PR #202, comment 6092559847, while adjudicating a builder's argument rather than taking it on trust. Related to #210 (a shared fill helper so a notebook and its test call one code path); this issue is the guard that the notebook calls it.

## The demonstration

Reviewing recipe 24, the reviewer deleted the `eval-test` cell's `submit_reviews` call, then **re-executed and committed exactly as a builder would**, and ran the full gate:

- `check_notebook_fresh.py` → `matches a fresh offline run`
- `pytest` → 38/38
- the recipe guard → only the known `next_steps_inbound_links` failure

All green, on a notebook that prints "review queue, both splits, 3 tickets" above three validation-only rows. So a recipe can ship a notebook whose stated behaviour contradicts its own output and pass every check we have.

## The two beliefs this falsifies

Both were offered in good faith as reasons the gap was already covered, and both are wrong:

1. **"The per-recipe `Notebook` CI job covers it."** It does not. That job catches a *stale* notebook — committed outputs that differ from a fresh offline run. A notebook re-executed after the edit is not stale; it is freshly and faithfully wrong. The job cannot distinguish a behaviour change from an intended one.
2. **"A `pytest` unit test cannot see an edit to notebook source."** Not true of this repository. `tests/test_recipe_guard.py::notebook_cells` already parses `notebook.ipynb`, and four of the fourteen per-recipe checks read it. The capability exists; nothing uses it for this.

## What to do

1. Add a per-recipe guard in `tests/test_recipe_guard.py`, in the same family as the existing `review_value_is_review` check: where a recipe's `helpers.py` defines a queue-submitting or other side-effect function, require the notebook source to call it. Parametrised over every published recipe, like the existing fourteen check ids, so a new recipe is covered as soon as it lands.
2. Settle how the guard identifies "the side effect" without being brittle. A named helper is detectable; an inline loop is not — which is the same force that makes #210 worth doing, and the two should be decided together. Recipe 24 is now the better-placed example because its side effect has a named helper a guard can look for; its siblings still inline the loop.
3. Decide what the guard does about a recipe whose side effect legitimately has no helper, so it fails closed on a real gap rather than on a shape it does not recognise.
4. Prove the guard by mutation, the way the gap was found: delete the notebook's call, re-execute, commit, and confirm the guard now fails where every existing check passed.
5. Audit the published recipes for the same latent gap and record the result here; fixes go through the normal reviewed pipeline.

Worth doing before more Level 3 and the nine `needs: simulator` recipes (#36, #43, #45, #46, #48, #57, #58, #59, #60) land with inline queue loops, since each one that ships widens the audit.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A parametrised guard exists in `tests/test_recipe_guard.py` requiring a notebook to invoke its recipe's side-effect helper.
- [ ] The guard's identification rule is written down and fails closed on an unrecognised shape.
- [ ] The guard is proved by the exact mutation above: delete the call, re-execute, commit, guard fails.
- [ ] Published recipes are audited for the gap and the result recorded here.
- [ ] The interaction with #210 is resolved deliberately, not left to whichever lands first.

title: Foundation: the glossary-linking rule has no guard, and the same finding has now hit three recipes
body:
The glossary-linking rule in `docs/recipe-template.md` (and `CONTRIBUTING.md` section 6) has no guard in `tests/test_recipe_guard.py`, so it drifts silently and every reviewer has to catch it by eye. Raised by the Opus review of PR #206 (comment 6092513082); it is not that review's to fix.

## Why now

The same class of finding appeared on **three different recipes within a few hours**, which `orchestration/PROMPT.md` treats as a signal that the fault is at the source rather than in any one recipe:

- **#204 / recipe 29** — must-change MC5: nine terms unlinked on first use (gold label, precision, recall, F1, support, confidence gate, provenance). A later suggestion on the same pull request found `accuracy` still unlinked in a sentence that links `coverage` and `risk`.
- **#202 / recipe 24** — original finding 7 came back only *partly* resolved: five links added, `gold label` still missing. The next round then wrote it as `` (`gold label`, ../../docs/glossary.md#gold-label) `` — a bare path, not a Markdown link, which renderers do not autolink. So a guard must check the **link form**, not merely that the anchor string appears somewhere in the cell.
- **#206 / recipe 26** — `f1` and `accuracy` unlinked.

Reviewers are currently the only enforcement, which is expensive, inconsistent between recipes, and will not scale to sixty.

## What to do

1. Decide and write down the actual rule, because "first use" needs a definition a check can apply: which terms are in scope (the template's lexicon, presumably), what counts as a first use (first markdown cell in notebook order? per notebook? does the recipe README count separately?), and what the required form is — a relative Markdown link such as `[gold label](../../docs/glossary.md#gold-label)`, matching what the published recipes already do.
2. Add the guard to `tests/test_recipe_guard.py`, parametrised over every published recipe the way the existing fourteen check ids are, so a new recipe is covered the moment it lands.
3. Make it catch the failure modes actually seen, not just the easy one: term absent entirely; anchor mentioned as a bare path rather than a link; link present but after the first use; anchor that does not exist in `docs/glossary.md`.
4. Fix the existing drift it finds across published recipes through the normal reviewed pipeline. Expect a backlog — treat the sweep as its own pull request, not as an addition to a recipe pull request open for another purpose.
5. If part of the rule genuinely cannot be checked mechanically, say so here and say what reviewers remain responsible for, so the boundary is explicit rather than assumed.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The rule is stated precisely enough to implement, in `docs/recipe-template.md` or `CONTRIBUTING.md`.
- [ ] `tests/test_recipe_guard.py` enforces it, parametrised over every published recipe.
- [ ] The guard fails on each of the four failure modes above; a test proves each.
- [ ] Every anchor a recipe links actually exists in `docs/glossary.md`.
- [ ] Existing drift across published recipes is enumerated here and fixed through its own reviewed pull request.
- [ ] Anything left to human judgement is written down as such.

title: Foundation: ReviewQueue and the simulation primitives need a shared fill helper so a notebook and its test call one code path
body:
Raised by the Opus re-review of PR #202 (recipe 24), comment 6092161895, as an observation belonging to the foundation rather than a defect in that recipe. Not blocking any open pull request.

## The problem

`jev_cookbook.simulation`'s `ReviewQueue` is easy to use from a notebook cell and hard to test from `tests/`. The only route a recipe has to assert on queue contents is to re-type the notebook's submission loop inside the test. That is not hypothetical: it is exactly how must-change finding 1 on #202 arose. The test there rebuilt the loop instead of calling the notebook's code, built its own `expected_order` inside that loop, and consequently passed under four separate mutations — dropping the validation loop, reversing the splits, adding the demo split, and deleting the notebook's entire `queue.submit` block all left it green at 38/38. A test that duplicates the behaviour it checks cannot check it.

The cost is about to multiply. Recipes 36, 43, 45, 46, 48, 57, 58, 59 and 60 all carry the `needs: simulator` flag and will build simulated side effects inline the same way, so whichever shape lands here is the shape nine more recipes copy. `orchestration/PROMPT.md` says a design question that would be costly to reverse across many recipes is decided once in the foundation and written into the docs — this is one.

## What to do

1. Give `jev_cookbook.simulation` a helper that takes the outcomes and fills the queue, so a notebook cell and its test call **one** code path instead of two copies. Settle the shape deliberately: what it accepts, what it returns, how the ordering and the per-item reason string are determined, and how a recipe excludes a demo or held-out case.
2. Make that path assertable without re-typing it: a recipe's test should be able to state the expected ids, count, order and split membership as literals and compare against the helper's own output.
3. Decide the same question for any other `simulation` primitive a recipe currently has to drive with an inline loop, so the answer is consistent rather than per-recipe.
4. Write the convention into `docs/simulation.md` and the recipe template, with a short worked example, so the next nine builders inherit it instead of improvising.
5. Add a guard or test that a published recipe's simulated-side-effect test actually exercises the shared path, or record here why that cannot be checked mechanically.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A documented helper exists, with its own tests, that both a notebook and a recipe test can call as the single code path.
- [ ] A recipe test can pin expected ids, count, order and both-split membership independently of the submission loop.
- [ ] `docs/simulation.md` and the recipe template carry the convention and a worked example.
- [ ] The interface is reviewed against the nine `needs: simulator` recipes (#36, #43, #45, #46, #48, #57, #58, #59, #60) rather than against recipe 24 alone.
- [ ] A guard or test prevents a recipe from reverting to a duplicated inline loop, or this issue records why not.

title: Foundation: the scaffold makes all sixty recipes import the private jev_cookbook.live._dump; promote it to public API
body:
Found by the Opus review of PR #204 (recipe 29), comment 6092133307, reported as belonging to a different issue rather than to that recipe. Not a blocker for any open pull request.

## The problem

`tests/test_build_fixtures.py` in a scaffolded recipe imports `jev_cookbook.live._dump`. The reviewer verified that the generated file is byte-identical to `tools/new_recipe.py::build_fixtures_test_text`, so this is not one builder's shortcut: the scaffolder requires **every one of the sixty recipes** to import a private, underscore-prefixed name from the shared package.

That is wrong in both directions. A leading underscore tells a reader the name is internal and may change without notice, yet sixty recipes and their tests depend on it — so it is in practice public API carrying a private name. Any future change to `_dump` breaks sixty test files at once, and a reader learning from a recipe is being shown that reaching into another module's privates is normal practice.

## What to do

1. Give the behaviour a public name in `jev_cookbook.live` (or wherever it belongs), documented and covered by its own test.
2. Update `tools/new_recipe.py::build_fixtures_test_text` so newly scaffolded recipes import the public name.
3. Migrate the already-published recipes that import `_dump`. Enumerate them first: `git grep -n '_dump' -- 'recipes/*' 'src/' 'tools/'`.
4. Decide deliberately whether `_dump` stays as a thin alias for compatibility or is removed outright, and record the decision. Nothing here weakens or skips a check.
5. Note the interface question the fix should answer while it is open: is dumping fixture responses the recipes' concern at all, or should the shared package expose a single "write these responses" helper the test asserts against? Sixty recipes copy whatever shape is chosen, which is why this is a foundation decision and not a tidy-up.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A public, documented helper exists with its own test.
- [ ] `tools/new_recipe.py` generates the public import, and a scaffold test proves it.
- [ ] Every published recipe importing `_dump` is migrated, with the enumeration recorded here.
- [ ] The keep-or-remove decision for `_dump` is recorded, and if it stays, what it is for.
- [ ] No recipe imports an underscore-prefixed shared name afterwards, enforced by a guard or test where practical.

title: Foundation: a fixed-order Choice must print no first-option-lean statistic; brief and docs contradict each other
body:
Found by the Opus review of PR #204 (recipe 29), comment 6092133307, as must-change finding MC2. Filed here because the cause is upstream of that recipe and will keep reproducing in every remaining `Choice` recipe if it is only fixed in recipe 29.

## The defect

Recipe 29's notebook prints the share of gold answers that fall on the first listed option and frames it as a check for a model's first-option lean — "not disproportionate the way a strong first-option lean would make it". Offline, that share is a property of the builder's own hand-written fixtures and nothing else. It cannot say anything about any model's position bias, so the sentence is a claim about Jev's behaviour unsupported by any recorded run, which section 2 of `CONTRIBUTING.md` forbids.

## Why it is a foundation issue, not a recipe fix

PR #204's description attributes the design to "the build notes": a choice between "a printed gold-position table with per-item shuffling" and "a fixed order with the first-option lean printed". Issue #29's Build notes contain nothing of the sort. Meanwhile `docs/fixtures.md` ("Per-item option order") and `docs/recipe-template.md` line 157 say the opposite — that a `Choice` with a fixed, meaningful option order "needs none of this". So a builder is receiving an instruction that contradicts the documentation, and the orchestration brief is the likeliest source.

## What to do

1. Find where that instruction originates — an orchestration brief, the recipe template, the scaffolder's generated prose, or `docs/` — and remove or correct it so a fixed meaningful order needs no position statistic at all.
2. Make `docs/fixtures.md` and `docs/recipe-template.md` unambiguous on the point: when per-item option order matters, use the seeded permutation helper from #181 and say what it does; when the order is fixed and meaningful, print no position statistic, because offline it measures only the fixture author.
3. State the general rule once, where reviewers will find it: no statistic computed from synthetic fixtures may be described as evidence about the model. Numbers from a synthetic run are pipeline checks and must be labelled so beside each number.
4. **Audit the already-merged recipes.** `git grep -i -e 'first option' -e 'first-option' -e 'lean' -e 'position bias' -- 'recipes/*/notebook.ipynb'` on `main` hits recipes 01, 02 and 18. Determine for each whether it makes the same unsupported claim or is innocent wording, and list the result here. Any real instance is fixed through the normal reviewed pipeline, not inside a recipe pull request that is open for another purpose.
5. Tell the builders still running on `Choice` recipes, so they do not repeat it.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The originating instruction is located and corrected, with the location named in a comment here.
- [ ] `docs/fixtures.md` and `docs/recipe-template.md` agree, and neither can be read as asking for a first-option-lean print on a fixed-order `Choice`.
- [ ] The "no model claim from synthetic statistics" rule is stated in a place reviewers already read.
- [ ] Recipes 01, 02 and 18 are audited with the per-recipe verdict recorded here; any genuine instance has its own tracked fix.
- [ ] A test or guard prevents the regression, or this issue records explicitly why one is not practical.

title: Recipe guard: inbound Next-steps link check cannot pass on a new recipe's PR; make it a wave close-out audit
body:
`tests/test_recipe_guard.py::test_every_recipe_is_linked_from_some_other_recipes_next_steps` (check `next_steps_inbound_links`, from #165 / #76 comment 6079429778) asserts that some other published recipe's Next steps links to each recipe. A new recipe's pull request can never satisfy it: no recipe on `main` may link forward to a recipe that does not exist yet (`next_steps_links_exist` forbids it), and a recipe PR may change only its own folder (`Scope`). PR #202 (recipe 24) is the first affected: it is the only failing test in the full suite on both Pythons. Every Wave 3 recipe PR will fail the same way, and the empty allowlist must stay empty.

Proposed change (small, test-only plus docs):
- Mark that one test with a registered pytest marker `catalog_audit` and deselect the marker by default in `pyproject.toml` (`addopts = "--import-mode=importlib -m 'not catalog_audit'"`), so per-PR CI no longer runs it.
- The wave close-out runs it explicitly: `pytest -m catalog_audit tests/test_recipe_guard.py`; the close-out sweep adds the missing backlinks. Document this in `docs/development.md` ("Continuous integration") and in the guard module docstring's scope decisions; keep the test itself and its message unchanged.
- Prove in the PR that the default collection excludes exactly that test and that `-m catalog_audit` selects it (`--collect-only -q` output in the PR comment), and that the full suite is otherwise unchanged (same counts minus 23 parametrised cases).

Alternatives considered and rejected: exempting the newest recipe couples every Wave 3 PR to the previous one's merge order; letting a recipe PR edit an earlier recipe's Next steps breaks the scope rule and forces a re-execution outside the PR's folder.

title: Foundation: stable seeded permutation helper for per-item option order
body:
From the recipe 12 re-review (PR #170, comment 6077517964). `random.shuffle` is not a documented-stable algorithm across CPython versions, yet `ScriptedBackend.rng_for` and recipe-local shuffles (recipe 12's `shuffled_candidates`) make committed replay keys depend on it; today only byte-reproduction tests on 3.10/3.14 cover it.

Acceptance: a documented helper in the shared package (e.g. `jev_cookbook.fixtures.stable_permutation(seed_key, n)` using a Fisher–Yates over a seeded `random.Random` whose `random()` sequence is documented-stable, or an explicit hash-derived permutation), tested to a pinned expected permutation for fixed keys; `docs/fixtures.md` tells recipe authors to use it for per-item option order; `ScriptedBackend.rng_for` callers reviewed. Recipe 12's local shuffle migrates in a later recipe-side sweep (#163). Allowed paths: `src/jev_cookbook/`, `tests/`, `docs/fixtures.md`, `docs/backends.md`. Split out of #161.

title: Foundation: single-option Choice confidence convention and cross-split replay-key leak check
body:
Found in the recipe 14 review (PR #173, comment 6075771134).

1. `choice_confidence` returns 1.0 for a single-option `Choice` where the published formula `(p_max − 1/n)/(1 − 1/n)` is 0/0, and `Choice` accepts one option. Decide the convention once: reject `n == 1` at build time (preferred — a forced answer belongs to Python, not a request), or document the special case in `docs/evaluation.md` and the confidence page reference. Add a test either way.

2. The fixture validator's leak rule compares `state`/`fields` across splits, so two splits can share an identical replay key unreported (recipe 14's `v17` and `t15` shared key `086703a0…`). Compare `replay_keys` across `validation`/`test` as well and report the pair.

Tracked from #80.

title: Foundation: selective_curve yields duplicate candidate thresholds from float-unequal Noul complements
body:
Found in the recipe 15 review (PR #169, comment 6075296491).

`noul_confidence` is mirror-symmetric for one `p` and its computed complement, but two separately stored nominal complements (e.g. `0.93` and `0.07` as independent floats) produce `0.8600000000000001` and `0.8599999999999999`. `selective_curve` then emits two distinct candidate thresholds that print identically (`gate >= 0.86` twice), and any Noul three-path recipe (02, 10, 15 and every later one) shows the duplicate row.

Proposed fix in `src/jev_cookbook/evaluation.py`: round confidences to a fixed number of decimals (e.g. 12) inside `noul_confidence`/`_conf_inputs` before candidate thresholds are taken, or dedupe candidates in `selective_curve` by rounded value; add a test with two stored complements that differ in the last ulp. Document the rounding in `docs/evaluation.md`. No recipe change is needed once the shared helper rounds.

Tracked from #80.

title: tests: parametrise the recipe fixture-builder guard over published recipes and drop the per-recipe copies
body:
## Context

From the Wave 1 consistency review: `tests/test_build_fixtures.py` is nine byte-identical 88-line copies across recipes 01, 03–10 (recipe 02 has none), and nothing documents the file. `tests/test_recipe_sources.py` already shows the pattern: one parametrised test over the published recipes.

## Acceptance

1. `tests/test_recipe_build_fixtures.py`: for every published recipe, import its `build_fixtures.py` and assert the three guards (refusal without `--force` when a response is `recorded`, inputs/labels regenerated during a refused run, writer byte-identical to `jev_cookbook.live._dump`) plus byte-identical regeneration; mutation-proven on one recipe.
2. Remove the per-recipe copies (keeping only genuinely recipe-specific assertions), update the template and scaffolder so new recipes stop shipping the copy (coordinate with #162's template test), and document the guard in `docs/recipe-template.md`.

Foundation issue; allowed paths `tests/test_recipe_build_fixtures.py` (new), `recipes/*/tests/test_build_fixtures.py` (deletions/trims), `recipes/_template/tests/*`, `tools/new_recipe.py`, `docs/recipe-template.md`. Starts after #162 merges.

title: Template/docs follow-ups from the Wave 1 consistency review: recipe-level fixture guard, glossary terms, print-what-you-plot, review value, lexicon
body:
## Context

Template/docs findings from the Wave 1 consistency review (orchestrator relay on #80, 2026-10-09), after #162 (closes #137) lands. The template is the standard, so every rule it embodies must be written in `docs/` with a test that applies to recipes, not only to `recipes/_template`.

Strengthen `test_stored_answers_are_not_all_right` (template + scaffolder) to require at least one wrong answer at or above the frozen threshold, and make a parametrised recipe-level version run over every published recipe (`tests/test_recipe_fixtures.py`, modelled on `tests/test_recipe_sources.py`).

title: Wave 1 recipe-side follow-ups: selection labels, evaluate_outcomes swap, guard-test assertion, dead bindings, README alignment
body:

title: evaluation: multi-label pooling and outcome-tally helpers; three-path docs caveats; hygiene generic username 'agent'
body:
## Context

From the Opus review of #158 (recipe 06, the first multi-label Noul recipe; comment 6073874449). The recipe hand-rolled two helpers in the notebook — `pooled_correct_and_confidence` (pool (example, label) pairs into the correctness/confidence arrays the three-path pattern needs) and `tally_outcomes` (tally a multi-label rule's own outcomes) — which every later multi-label Noul recipe will re-implement.

## Acceptance

1. `jev_cookbook.evaluation` gains documented helpers for multi-label Noul recipes: pooling (example, label) decisions into flat `correct`/`confidence` arrays (with label attribution kept, e.g. returning a list of (example_id, label) keys alongside), and an outcomes tally compatible with `evaluate_outcomes` (#155) — both tested, with an identity check against the hand-rolled versions in recipe 06 once merged.
2. `docs/evaluation.md` "Noul three-path pattern": state that when the confidence gate is the rule's only review branch, `evaluate_selective` and an outcome tally give the same numbers; promote the "distance from 0.5, not margin at the threshold" caveat for per-label-threshold recipes (the gate is structurally blind to errors just below a high threshold).
3. `tools/check_hygiene.py`: `_GENERIC_USERNAMES` lacks `agent` (this container's account name), so ordinary English words trip the local-username rule in printed notebook output; add it (and any other common-word account names) without weakening the rule for real usernames; test.
4. Docs note for `noul_confidence`: two decimal literals that are mathematical mirrors (0.42 / 0.58) differ by 1 ULP, so `selective_curve` can yield two adjacent candidates for one nominal confidence; mention it where mirrored hand-written probabilities are discussed.

Foundation issue; allowed paths `src/jev_cookbook/evaluation.py`, `tests/test_evaluation*.py`, `docs/evaluation.md`, `tools/check_hygiene.py`, `tests/test_check_hygiene*.py`. Starts after #160 merges; required before the later multi-label recipes (#25 and others) are briefed.

title: docs: merge-readiness record corrections (model id, missing file reference, stale sentences) and the description-edit rule in CONTRIBUTING
body:
## Context

Documentation nits collected by the Opus reviews of #154 (comment 6073518690) and earlier helper reviews; none blocks a merge, all are in `docs/merge-readiness.md` or `CONTRIBUTING.md`.

## Acceptance

title: evaluation: guard select_confidence_threshold inputs; document selective metrics for rules with an option-based review branch
body:
## Context

From the reviews of #153 (recipe 09; comment 6072191186) and #148 (recipe 07): a Choice rule whose review branch is an option (`unsorted`, `unclear`, a foreign option) has no documented convention in `jev_cookbook.evaluation`. Recipes invent a sentinel confidence (recipe 09's `placement_confidence` returns −1.0; recipe 07 uses 0.0) so `evaluate_selective` reproduces the rule's split. With a −1.0 sentinel, `select_confidence_threshold` happily returns a candidate outside [0, 1] when the target accuracy admits every answer, and the rule then raises on `min_confidence` validation.

## Acceptance

1. `select_confidence_threshold` validates its inputs: confidences outside [0, 1] raise a clear `ValueError` (so sentinels cannot leak into a threshold), with a test.
2. `docs/evaluation.md` documents the convention for rules with an option-based review branch: compute selective metrics from the rule's own outcomes (a short helper `selective_from_outcomes(accepted: list[bool], correct: list[bool])` returning coverage/accuracy/risk is acceptable if trivial and tested), and never feed sentinels into the selectors; the template's sentence "`evaluate_selective` reports the same split" is qualified accordingly (`docs/recipe-template.md`).
3. Recipes 07 and 09 are adjusted to the documented convention in their own PRs (if still open) or in a follow-up.

Foundation issue; allowed paths `src/jev_cookbook/evaluation.py`, `tests/test_evaluation*.py`, `docs/evaluation.md`, `docs/recipe-template.md`.

title: evaluation: noul_confidence must be |2p − 1| per the confidence page (same scale as Choice); document the Noul three-path pattern
body:
## Context

From the Opus review of #136 (recipe 02, the first Noul recipe; comment 6071121590). `src/jev_cookbook/evaluation.py` and `docs/evaluation.md` define `noul_confidence(p) = max(p, 1 − p)` (range 0.5–1). The TypeSafe confidence page (`https://docs.typesafe.ai/confidence.md`, README S03) defines a Noul's confidence as `|2p − 1|` (range 0–1) and states it is the Choice formula `(p_max − 1/n)/(1 − 1/n)` applied with n = 2, so it sits on the same scale as Choice confidence. The toolkit helper therefore disagrees with the source, and a recipe that gates Nouls and Choices with one threshold, as the page recommends, gets wrong answers from it. `docs/evaluation.md` documents the Choice rescaling correctly on the same page.

## Acceptance

1. `noul_confidence(p)` returns `|2p − 1|` per the confidence page (the old `max(p, 1 − p)` is removed or kept under a distinct, documented name such as `noul_majority`); `docs/evaluation.md` and `docs/glossary.md` state the formula with the source link and note the shared scale with Choice.
2. Tests pin the formula at p ∈ {0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1} and the identity with `(p_max − 1/n)/(1 − 1/n)` at n = 2; mutation: revert to `max(p, 1 − p)` → tests fail.
3. Every call site in `src/`, `recipes/_template`, `tools/new_recipe.py` and merged recipes is checked; any notebook whose outputs change is re-executed and committed byte-identically in the same PR (list them).
4. Add to `docs/evaluation.md` a short "Noul three-path pattern" note: a business threshold on p plus a confidence gate `|2p − 1| < c` → review outcome, composed from `threshold_sweep` / `evaluate_threshold`, since no helper selects both together (the Score recipes reported the same gap).

Required before the remaining Noul recipes (#6, #10, and later waves) are briefed. Foundation issue; allowed paths `src/jev_cookbook/evaluation.py`, `tests/test_evaluation*.py`, `docs/evaluation.md`, `docs/glossary.md`, plus re-executed notebooks only if their outputs change.

title: Readiness helper: duplicate successful Scope rows on one head (synchronize + edited) fail closed; decide the rule
body:
## Context

Found by governance on #133 (comment 6071008435; receipt `goal-handoffs/01a11360-…-133-duplicate-scope-not-ready-receipt.json`) and reproduced by the orchestrator: head `d4df2c2` carried two successful `Scope (recipe pull requests)` CheckRuns (runs 37858946288 from `synchronize` and 37858968112 from `edited`, both `SUCCESS`). The #118 helper, as accepted, fails closed on duplicate results for a required head check: `head: duplicate results (2) for check: Scope (recipe pull requests)`, exit 1. `scope.yml` runs on `pull_request_target` for `opened`, `synchronize`, `reopened` and `edited`, so any description edit after the last push creates the pair. For recipe pull requests `Scope` is head-required, so the gate would be unreachable whenever a builder PATCHes the description after pushing.

## Decision wanted (reviewed, not a workaround)

Pick one, with tests either way:

1. **Helper**: when several completed CheckRuns share a required head name on the same head commit, treat them as one result if and only if every one of them concluded `success`; any other mix (any failure, cancelled, pending, or differing conclusions) still fails closed as today. Document the rule in `docs/merge-readiness.md`. Mutation: two success rows → READY; success + cancelled → NOT READY; success + pending → NOT READY.
2. **Workflow**: make `scope.yml` idempotent per head so a second run supersedes the first (GitHub keeps both CheckRuns; a `concurrency` group with `cancel-in-progress` leaves a `cancelled` row, which also fails closed), so option 1 is likely still needed.

Interim process rule (in force now, recorded on #80): no description edits after the final push of a head going to the gate; receipts go in comments. Allowed paths: `tools/check_merge_readiness.py`, `tests/test_merge_readiness.py`, `docs/merge-readiness.md` (option 1) and/or `.github/workflows/scope.yml`, `tests/test_notebook_ci_workflows.py`, `docs/notebook-ci.md` (option 2). Foundation issue; owner to be assigned by the orchestrator (support lane acceptable under the READY rule).

title: Template and scaffold follow-ups from the recipe 01 reviews (before the recording wave)
body:
## Context

Both Opus review seats on #123 (recipe 01, the reference recipe; comments 6058687733 and 6058612766) reported defects that live in the template, the scaffold, or the shared package rather than in the recipe. Fifty-nine more recipes are scaffolded from these, and recipe 01 is the first recording target, so they should land before the recording wave.

## Scaffold (`tools/new_recipe.py`)

1. `build_fixtures.py` from the scaffold uses one `ROWS` table, so inputs/labels cannot be regenerated without rewriting `responses.json`; one `python build_fixtures.py` after a live recording silently overwrites `recorded` responses with synthetic probabilities. Add `--inputs-only` / `--responses-only` (or refuse to overwrite a file whose provenance is `recorded`).
2. The `--mode replay` test skeleton ships a dead scripted branch reading `helpers.script` / `helpers.SEED`; recipe 01 copied it verbatim.
3. The scaffolded README "Switch to live" section omits `JEV_COOKBOOK_LIVE_MAX_REQUESTS` and does not state the request count against the default budget of 25.
4. `build_fixtures.py` writes `responses.json` unsorted while the recorder writes it sorted; pick one order so a recording produces a minimal diff.

## Template (`recipes/_template`)

5. The "What was and was not measured" markdown cell is hardcoded prose beside a mode-derived code cell; once `responses.json` is swapped for recorded answers the notebook executes green with stale prose. Derive the markdown's claims from `backend.mode` too, or move the claim entirely into the code cell. It also counts `demo` examples in N ("22 invented messages" where 20 are scored).
6. The `check` suffix on numbers is mode-gated, so a recorded recipe prints validation accuracy bare; CONTRIBUTING §2 treats a validation number as a selection step, not a result. Make the selection-step wording unconditional.

title: Foundation: hygiene scanner flags long keyword arguments of the form name=CONSTANT as high-entropy tokens

title: Foundation: catalog sync inside recipe pull requests (resolve the README check conflict)
body:
## Goal

Make the rules about recipe pull requests, the README catalog, and CI hold at the same time, before the first recipe lands.

## The conflict

Today these four rules cannot all be true:

- A recipe pull request touches only `recipes/NN-slug/` (`CONTRIBUTING.md`, orchestration rule 5).
- Adding `recipes/NN-slug/notebook.ipynb` flips that recipe to published in `tools/render_catalog.py`.
- The `Catalog (README is current)` check on every pull request requires `README.md` to match the catalog render immediately (#62).
- The README is regenerated only in one catalog sync pull request after each wave (orchestration rule 6).

So every recipe pull request would fail the catalog check, and the only ways out are a red check, a disabled check, or a stale README, all of which the rules forbid.

## Resolution (decided by the orchestrator, 2026-10-06)

- Recipe builders stay confined to `recipes/NN-slug/`.
- As the last step before final review, after the branch has been updated against current `main`, a designated integration step runs `python tools/render_catalog.py` and commits only the resulting change to the generated regions of `README.md` into the same recipe pull request. This step is serialized across recipe pull requests by the orchestrator, so the regenerated README is always based on current `main`.
- A recipe pull request may therefore change exactly two things: its own `recipes/NN-slug/` folder, and the generated regions of `README.md`. Nothing else, and never hand-written README prose.
- The catalog check stays strict and unchanged. No recipe merges with the README stale.
- The per-wave catalog sync pull request is no longer needed for publication status; after each wave the orchestrator only verifies the README links and counts.

## Scope

- `CONTRIBUTING.md`: replace the "touches only `recipes/NN-slug/`" wording with the two-things rule above, say who runs the renderer and when, and say that hand edits to `README.md` are still forbidden.
- `orchestration/PROMPT.md`: update rules 5 and 6, the "After each recipe wave" section, and the builder brief to match; also update rules 3 and 4 to point at the owner's live-inference decision recorded on #80 (live recording is authorized within $25 total, only after #64 merges, with `recorded` provenance only for real API responses).
- `docs/development.md`: a short section on the catalog regions and the integration step.
- `tools/render_catalog.py`: no behaviour change. If a `--diff` or `--check` improvement is needed to make the integration step verifiable, keep it minimal and tested.
- A tested helper or documented command that verifies a recipe pull request's diff is confined to `recipes/NN-slug/` plus the generated README regions, so #69 can use it as its scope check. Keep it small; #69 wires it into CI.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `CONTRIBUTING.md`, `orchestration/PROMPT.md`, and `docs/development.md` describe the same rule, with no leftover mention of a per-wave catalog sync as the way recipes get published
- [ ] The scope helper accepts a diff touching `recipes/NN-slug/**` plus generated README regions, and rejects a diff touching README prose, another recipe, shared code, or the catalog; tests prove both
- [ ] `python tools/render_catalog.py --check` still passes on `main`
- [ ] Lint, tests, and the hygiene check pass in CI

## Dependencies

- Blocks the first recipe (#1). Must merge before #69 wires the scope check into CI.
- Tracked in #74

## References

- Orchestrator decision record on #80: https://github.com/Jev-Engineering/cookbook/issues/80#issuecomment-6025510672
- `tools/render_catalog.py` and its tests in `tests/test_render_catalog.py` (#62)

title: Cookbook roadmap: 60 recipes from foundation to release
body:
The whole build in one place: sixty recipes, the foundation they stand on, and the release audit.

## Plan

| Wave | Tracking issue | Issues | Milestone |
| :---: | --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | #74 Foundation | #61 to #72 | M0 · Foundation |
| 1 | #75 Level 1 · Beginner | #1 to #10 | M1 · Beginner |
| 2 | #76 Level 2 · Easy | #11 to #23 | M2 · Easy |
| 3 | #77 Level 3 · Intermediate | #24 to #39 | M3 · Intermediate |
| 4 | #78 Level 4 · Advanced | #40 to #52 | M4 · Advanced |
| 5 | #79 Level 5 · Expert | #53 to #60 | M5 · Expert |
| 6 | #73 Release 1.0 audit | #73 | Release 1.0 |

**Recipe N is issue #N.** Issues #1 to #60 are the recipes in catalog order.

## How the issues are triaged

- **Type**: `type: recipe`, `type: foundation`, `type: epic`.
- **Level, category, decision type**: taken from the catalog, so the issue list can be filtered into a learning track.
- **Priority**: `p0` blocks everything, `p1` is the next wave, `p2` and `p3` follow. Priority follows the dependency order, not importance.
- **Size**: `S` about half a day, `M` about a day, `L` two to three days, `XL` several days. Estimates, to be corrected as work lands.
- **Status**: `status: ready` means no open blockers. `status: blocked` means the Dependencies section lists what it waits for. `status: in progress` and `status: needs human` are set during the build.
- **Needs**: `needs: simulator` waits for the simulation primitives. `needs: live run` marks recipes whose real conclusions need recorded live inference.
- **Dependencies** are also recorded as GitHub issue dependencies, and every issue is a sub-issue of its tracking issue.

## Ground rules

- The [recipe contract](https://github.com/Jev-Engineering/cookbook/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md) defines done for a recipe.
- The [orchestration prompt](https://github.com/Jev-Engineering/cookbook/blob/main/orchestration/PROMPT.md) describes how the build is run with agents.
- Recipe pull requests touch only their own folder. The README is regenerated from the catalog, one sync per wave.
- Nothing merges on a red or pending check.

## Goal

Shared building blocks for recipes that keep state or run a loop, so thirteen advanced recipes do not each invent a queue and a simulator.

## Scope

- A deterministic, seeded simulator base: reset, observe, enumerate legal actions, step, and a trajectory log that can be replayed.
- A simulated review queue and action log, used wherever a recipe says an item goes to review or an action is simulated.
- A versioned key-value store that keeps provenance and never deletes, with history and rollback.
- A transactional wrapper: validate, apply, roll back on failure, with a replayable log.

- Guidance on using `ScriptedBackend` to run a closed loop offline.

title: Foundation: evaluation toolkit
body:
## Goal

Shared, tested metrics so recipes report results the same way and no notebook reimplements a confusion matrix.

## Scope

- Choice: accuracy, per-class precision, recall and F1, macro and micro averages, confusion matrix, Cohen's kappa.
- Noul: precision and recall at a threshold, threshold sweep, threshold selection on a validation split, Brier score.
- Multi-label: per-label and micro and macro F1, exact-set match.
- Score and ranking: exact agreement, mean absolute error, nDCG, top-k accuracy, recall at a budget.
- Selective prediction: accuracy against coverage, risk and coverage curve, threshold selection that is frozen before test.
- Calibration: reliability table and expected calibration error.
- Comparison: paired bootstrap confidence interval for the difference between two systems.
- Accounting: request counts and token usage summed from `usage`.
- Plain `numpy`. Each function has a docstring that says what it measures in one sentence.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Every metric has tests against small hand-computed cases, including edge cases (empty class, all one label, ties)
- [ ] Functions accept the typed answer objects from the backends issue as well as plain arrays
- [ ] No metric silently returns a number for empty input
- [ ] Lint and tests pass in CI, or locally with the output pasted in the pull request if CI does not exist yet

## Goal

One fixture format across sixty recipes, checked by a tool, so fixtures stay readable and honest.

## Scope

- A written specification for `fixtures/`: inputs, gold labels, and model responses, in JSON or JSON Lines, with stable identifiers linking the three.
